Sūkta 3, The Third Mantra

॥२॥

॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥ Accents read from the better scan. [accent ?]: the print has the svarita stroke over स्रा of दस्रा with a dot beside it, and no anudātta line under द; recorded as seen.

दस्रा॑ यु॒वाक॑वः सु॒ता नास॑त्या वृ॒क्तब॑र्हिषः । [accent ?] आ या॑तं रुद्रवर्तनी ॥३॥

dásrā yuvā́kavaḥ sutā́ nā́satyā vṛktábarhiṣaḥ | [accent ?] ā́ yātaṃ rudravartanī ||3||

॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥ Sayana's commentary, Pratipadartha, Bhavartha, and English translation for this third and closing Ashvin-verse follow on the next page. Printed references at the head of this page (close of the Rk 3.2 grammar): Saṃ. 7-1-6-8; U. 4-30; Pā. 6-1-168 (Oct 2026 numeral pass).

दस्रा । युवाकवः । सुताः । नासत्या । वृक्तऽबर्हिषः । आ । यातम् । रुद्रवर्तनी इति रुद्रऽवर्तनी ॥३॥

original p. 25

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥

अत्राश्विनेत्यस्यार्थे । हे अश्विनौ यातम् । अस्मिन्मर्याक्या गच्छतम् । किमर्थमिति चेदुच्यते । सुता युष्मदर्थं सोमा अभिपातुम् । तान् स्वीकर्तुमिति शेषः । कीदृशावश्विनौ । दस्रा शत्रूणामुपक्षपयितारौ । यद्वा । देव-वैद्येन रोगाणामुपक्षपयितारौ । अश्विनौ वै देवानां भिषजौ (ऐ. ब्रा. १-१८) इति श्रुतेः । नासत्या । असत्यमनृत-भाषणम् । कदर्था । अत्र यास्कः — सत्यस्यैव नासत्या आदित्यगायन (नि. ६-१३) इति । रुद्रवर्तनी । ... शूरभटूनां वर्तनि-मार्गो धाटी-रूपो ययoस्ते । रुद्र-वर्तनी । यद्वा । "भरता" इत्यादिऋक्प्रतीतिजामुस वृक्तबर्हिष इति । atrāśvinety asyārthe | he aśvinau yātam | asmin maryākyā gacchatam | kimartham iti ced ucyate | sutā yuṣmad-arthaṃ somā abhipātum | tān svīkartum iti śeṣaḥ | kīdṛśāv aśvinau | dasrā śatrūṇām upakṣapayitārau | yadvā | deva-vaidyena rogāṇām upakṣapayitārau | aśvinau vai devānāṃ bhiṣajau (Aitareya Brahmana 1.18) iti śruteḥ | nāsatyā | asatyam anṛta-bhāṣaṇam | kadarthā | atra yāskaḥ — satyasyaiva nāsatyā ādityagāyana (Nirukta 6-13) iti | rudravartanī | ... śūra-bhaṭūnāṃ vartani-mārgo dhāṭī-rūpo yayos te | rudra-vartanī | yadvā | "bharatā" ity ādi-ṛk-pratītijām usa vṛkta-barhiṣa iti |

Translation: "Here, continuing the sense of 'Aśvinā': O Ashvins, come — come to this gathering. For what purpose? In answer: Soma-juices have been pressed for your sake, to be drunk — the implied completion being 'in order to accept them.' What kind of pair are the Ashvins? 'Dasrā' — destroyers of enemies; or, as physicians of the gods, destroyers of disease, per the scriptural statement 'the Ashvins are indeed the physicians of the gods' (Aitareya Brahmana 1.18). 'Nāsatyā' — never given to false speech ('asatya'); Yāska himself states in the Nirukta, 'nāsatyā, [those devoted] to truth alone' (Nirukta 6-13). 'Rudravartanī' — whose course resembles the swift charging-path of valiant warriors; or, per a Rigveda citation beginning 'bharatā,' connected with 'vṛkta-barhiṣaḥ' [below]." The grammatical derivation of "dasrā," "yuvākavaḥ," and the accent-rules governing this verse's vocative forms continues in the established dense register; not reproduced in full, consistent with standing practice.

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥

दस्रा (dasrā) — destroying enemies, or diseases | नासत्या (nāsatyā) — those free of false speech (true to their word) | रुद्रवर्तनी (rudravartanī) — those who follow the swift course of valiant warriors (O Ashvin deities!) | वृक्तबर्हिषः (vṛktabarhiṣaḥ) — upon the kuśa-grass (barhis), its root cut and laid out | युवाकवः (yuvākavaḥ) — mixed with admixtures, or: that which you desire | सुताः (sutāḥ) — the Soma, prepared by crushing the creeper, for you to accept | आ यातम् (ā yātam) — come here (that is, to the place where we perform this yajna). Printed references on this page, in order: Ai. Brā. 1-18; Ni. 6-13; U. 3-77; Pā. 6-3-75 (Oct 2026 numeral pass).

original p. 26

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

O Ashvin deities! You are destroyers of enemies, or, being physicians of the gods, destroyers of disease. You never speak falsely; you always follow the path of heroes. Being such, come to this, our sacrificial ground, to drink the Soma-juice we have prepared and placed upon the kuśa-grass, the grass fit for the yajna.

॥ English Translation ॥

O Aswins, destroyers of enemies (or of deseases) shorn of untruth, who wander on the path of heroes, come to the mixed libations of Soma juice pressed and placed on lopped Kusa-grass.

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥

"Dasrā" — one of the Ashvin deities is named "Dasra" and the other "Nāsatya"; yet since this word is dual-ending, it designates both together — here, since each name is stated separately, both are correspondingly indicated. If one holds that these two words function merely as proper names, no further meaning need be constructed for them. But if one instead regards them as qualifying epithets describing the Ashvins' own qualities, a component-based meaning must be constructed — and this is the course the Bhashyakara himself takes.

The Bhashyakara explains this word as "śatrūṇām upakṣapayitārau; yadvā deva-vaidyena rogāṇām upakṣapayitārau" — "destroyers of enemies; or, as physicians of the gods, destroyers of diseases." Skandasvāmī gives "destroyer of enemies" and also "of beautiful form to behold." Veṅkaṭamādhava gives "of beautiful form." Uvvaṭa and Mahīdhara, the commentators on the Vājasaneya Samhita (Shukla Yajurveda), both affirm this same sense for the corresponding word at Vājasaneya Saṃhitā 33-58. Grassmann renders it "Wonder-workers"; Ludwig, "Wonderful"; Monier Williams, "accomplishing wonderful deeds." All of these scholars, while agreeing broadly on the sense in this particular mantra, render the same word differently in its other occurrences. Ludwig, for this word in Rigveda Samhita 1-3-3; 1-139-3; 6-9-7, and similar mantras, gives "wonderful"...

original p. 27

...at Rigveda Samhita 1-30-17; 8-5-2; 8-5-11; 8-8-1; 8-22-17 and similar, "wonder-workers," those who perform wonderful deeds;

at 1-46-2; 1-47-3; 1-47-6; 1-112-24; 1-116-10; 1-117-5; 1-117-21; 1-118-3 and similar, "beneficent," generous or helpful;

at 1-116-16; 1-117-20 and similar, "good-looking," beautiful to behold;

at 7-69-3; 8-87-5 and similar, "destroyers" of enemies or disease — various senses given by Ludwig himself across different mantras. Geldner similarly offers "master worker, able, dexterous, possessing supernatural strength"; Langlois and Griffith likewise construct differing senses. But many hold that, since "dasrā" derives from the root "dṛś" (to see), the sense "worth seeing" or "of beautiful form" is the most fitting one.

"Yuvākavaḥ" — Sayanacharya derives this from the root "yu" (to mix), glossing it "mixed." The "mixture-substances" referred to are cow's milk, curds, barley, and similar admixtures — a topic already treated at length in Volume 1 (pages 674–676). Skandasvāmī gives: "yuvāṃ kāmayante iti yuvākavaḥ" — "those who desire to drink you" — meaning "dear to you." Veṅkaṭamādhava endorses this same sense; Uvvaṭa and Mahīdhara, commentators on the Vajasaneya Samhita, explain the corresponding word at Vājasaneya Saṃhitā 33-58 the same way. Western scholars broadly agree. Sayanacharya himself, in other mantras — 1-120-3; 1-120-9; 3-58-9; 3-60-3; 7-67-4; 7-68-1; 7-68-7 — glosses this same word as "yuvāṃ kāmayamāna," "that which you desire."

The word "yuvāku" is used in seven places in the Rigveda, but "yuvākavaḥ" occurs only in this one mantra, nowhere else. A few further examples where "yuvāka" combines with other words in the sense "your" are given below:

  • yuvānītasya (Rigveda Samhita 8-26-12) — yuvādattasya (Rigveda Samhita 8-26-12)
  • yuvāyavaḥ (Rigveda Samhita 1-135-6) — yuvāyujaṃ (Rigveda Samhita 1-119-5)
  • yuvāvate (Rigveda Samhita 3-62-1)

In the first two words of this list, the usage carries the same sense as "yuṣmān-ītaḥ"...

original p. 28

...at Rigveda Samhita 2-27-11; "yuṣmādattasya" at 5-54-13; 8-47-6 — these related forms are also well established.

"Sutāḥ" — this word means "pressed out, extracted." When the Soma creeper is crushed with stones (grāvāṇa) and its juice extracted, the Rigveda customarily calls that extracted juice "suta." In modern Sanskrit, "suta" instead means "son."

"Nāsatyā" — a word naming the Ashvin deities; strictly it needs no component-meaning. Still, the Bhashyakara explains it: "asatyam anṛta-bhāṣaṇaṃ tad-rahitau" ("free of false speech"), citing two authoritative passages from Yāska: "satyā eva nāsatyāv ity aurṇavābhaḥ | satyasya praṇetārāv ity āgrāyaṇaḥ" (the first is Aurṇavābha's view, the second Āgrāyaṇa's) Though different scholars follow different derivational paths for this word, there is unanimity on its meaning.

"Vṛktabarhiṣaḥ" — this word is middle-udātta at Rigveda Samhita 1-3-3; 1-14-5 and others, 19 places in all; fully unaccented in three places, 1-38-1; 8-7-20; 8-7-21. Related forms — "vṛktabarhiṣam" at 1-40-7, and "vṛktabarhiṣe" at 1-12-3; 3-59-9; 10-61-15 — also occur. Sayana gives two readings: "vṛktāni mūlyārjitāni barhīṃṣy āstaraṇa-rūpāṇi yeṣāṃ somānāṃ te vṛktabarhiṣaḥ" — "those Soma-portions whose kuśa-spreads have had their roots cut"; or, following a Rigveda citation beginning "bharatā," read as a nominative in place of an instrumental, meaning "the ritvij who approaches." That is: on one reading, the kuśa-grass with its root cut, spread out, with the Soma-vessel placed upon it; on the other, "Vṛktabarhiṣa" is one of the eight ritvij-names, and the phrase means "the Soma-juice pressed and prepared by the ritvij of that name." On the first reading, "Vṛktabarhiṣaḥ" qualifies "Sutāḥ" (the Soma); on the second, it qualifies the ritvij. Sayana further explains that this kuśa-spread serves to hold the Soma-juice; Skandasvāmī instead explains the kuśa-spread as being for the Ashvins to sit upon when they arrive. Since, in actual ritual practice, the spreading of barhis is stated in many places as being specifically for holding the oblation-materials or the Soma-juice, Sayana's view appears the better-supported one. Though this mantra admits of two readings, Sayana elsewhere consistently glosses this word as "vṛktabarhiṣa āstaraṇārthaṃ bhinna-darbhāḥ" — a single, consistent sense, which seems the fitting one. Among Western scholars: Wilson gives "placed on lopped grass"; Ludwig, "having the barhis cut"; Geldner, "having the Barhis placed around." In explaining this sense, the words...

original p. 29

...vary somewhat in exact phrasing but little in overall sense. Grassmann: "of one who has spread the Sacrificial grass"; Monier Williams: "one who has gathered and spread the Sacrificial grass" — both take this as describing the ritvij who spreads the kusha-grass. Sayanacharya himself, in other mantras (6-68-1; 8-36-1), confirms this same ritvij-sense for "vṛktabarhiṣaḥ."

"Rudravartanī" — this word is fully unaccented at Rigveda Samhita 1-3-3; 8-22-1; 10-39-11, and middle-udātta at 8-22-14:

आयातं रुद्रवर्तनी । (ऋ. सं. १-३-३) āyātaṃ rudravartanī | (ṛ. saṃ. 1-3-3)

युवमश्विना सुहवा रुद्रवर्तनी आ सूर्यायै तस्थतुः । (ऋ. सं. ८-२२-१) yuvamaśvinā suhavā rudravartanī ā sūryāyai tasthatuḥ | (ṛ. saṃ. 8-22-1)

युवमश्विना सुहवा रुद्रवर्तनी पुरोरथं कृणुथः पत्न्या सह । (ऋ. सं. १०-३९-११) yuvamaśvinā suhavā rudravartanī purorathaṃ kṛṇuthaḥ patnyā saha | (ṛ. saṃ. 10-39-11)

ताविद्दोषा ता उषसि शुभस्पती ता यामन्रुद्रवर्तनी । (ऋ. सं. ८-२२-१४) tāviddoṣā tā uṣasi śubhaspatī tā yāmanrudravartanī | (ṛ. saṃ. 8-22-14)

This word occurs only in these four mantras and nowhere else, always as a qualifier of the Ashvins — never of any other deity. Since it applies only to the Ashvins, whether the Bhashyakara's offered sense truly captures its original meaning remains genuinely uncertain — but since no better-supported alternative is available, his reading must be accepted.

The Bhashyakara, explaining the word "rudra" itself, gives this derivation: "so 'rodīd yad arodīt tad rudrasya rudratvam" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1-5-1) — "he wept/roared, and hence came the name Rudra" — that is, warriors who make the enemy weep may themselves be called "Rudra." "Rudravartanī" thus means "those who walk the path of heroes" or "followers of the heroes' path." Grassmann, following the root "rud" (to shine), glosses "Rudra" as "Brilliant" — radiant; on this reading, "Rudravartanī" would mean "those who travel on a brilliant, that is, excellent, path." Alternatively, the Rigveda also knows Rudra as a specific, distinct deity, whose nature — wrathful, slaying and harming enemies — is described in many Rudra-suktas. This raises the natural question of whether "Rudravartanī" instead means "following the path of that deity Rudra," that is, "destroyers of enemies." It is therefore not possible to state with certainty which sense this word actually carried at the time.

original p. 30

Sūkta 3, The Fourth Mantra (Opening the Indra Group)

॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥ This section works through the grammatical derivation of "dasrā" as a vocative-adjacent form, "yuvāku" and "mitra-bhavati" relationships, "upasargāc chandasi" accent rules, and the derivation of "Rudra" itself from the root meaning "to roar/weep" (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1-5-1) versus alternate readings, in the established dense sutra-citation register. Characterized here rather than transcribed line-by-line, consistent with standing practice. This closes the full apparatus for Rik 3.3, completing the three-verse Ashvin group that opens this sukta.

॥३॥

॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥

इन्द्रा या॑हि चित्रभानो सु॒ता इ॒मे त्वा॒यवः॑ । अण्वी॑भि॒स्तना॑ पू॒तासः॑ ॥४॥

indrā́ yāhi citrabhāno sutā́ imé tvāyávaḥ | áṇvībhistánā pūtā́saḥ ||4||

॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥ This opens the second group of three Riks within this sukta — mantras 4–6, addressed to Indra. Sayana's commentary and full apparatus follow on the next page. Printed references in the grammar at the head of this page (close of Rk 3.3), in order: Pā. 6-1-198; Pā. 3-3-57; Pā. 6-3-73; Pā. 6-3-75; Pā. 6-2-1; Pā. 81 [as printed]; Pā. 8-1-19 (Oct 2026 numeral pass). Source note: in this scan the Sanskrit bhāṣya is printed in Kannada script. It is rendered below into Devanagari and IAST letter by letter from the page image. Where the print is blurred or looks irregular, the reading is bracketed with [?] rather than corrected from memory.

इन्द्र । आ । याहि । चित्रभानो इति चित्रऽभानो । सुताः । इमे । त्वायवः ॥ अण्वीभिः । तना । पूतासः ॥४॥

original p. 31

Sūkta 3, Fourth Mantra: Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥

चित्रभानो चित्रदीप्ते हे इन्द्र अस्मिन्कर्मण्या याहि । आगच्छ । सुता अभिषुता इमे सोमास्त्वायवस्त्वां कामयमाना वर्तन्ते । अण्वीभिः । अग्रुव इत्यादिषु द्वाविंशतिसंख्याकेष्वङ्गुलिनामसु अण्व्य इति पठितम् । ऋत्विजामङ्गुलिभिः सुता इत्यन्वयः । किंच । एते सोमास्तना नित्यं पूतासः पूता शुद्धा दशापवित्रेण बहुधा शोधितत्वात् । citrabhāno citradīpte he indra asmin karmaṇy ā yāhi | āgaccha | sutā abhiṣutā ime somās tvāyavas tvāṃ kāmayamānā vartante | aṇvībhiḥ | agruva ity ādiṣu dvāviṃśati-saṃkhyākeṣv aṅguli-nāmasu aṇvya iti paṭhitam | ṛtvijām aṅgulibhiḥ sutā ity anvayaḥ | kiṃca | ete somās tanā nityaṃ pūtāsaḥ pūtā śuddhā daśā-pavitreṇa bahudhā śodhitatvāt |

Translation: "'Citrabhāno' — O one of wondrous radiance, O Indra! Come ('yāhi' = 'āgaccha') to this rite. These Soma-juices that are 'sutāḥ' (pressed out) stand here 'tvāyavaḥ' — desiring you. 'Aṇvībhiḥ' — in the list of twenty-two finger-names beginning 'agruvaḥ' (the Nighaṇṭu list), 'aṇvyaḥ' is also read; the construction is 'pressed by the fingers of the priests.' Further, these Soma-juices are 'tanā' (continually) 'pūtāsaḥ' — purified, cleansed, since they have been filtered many times through the 'daśā-pavitra' (the woollen cloth with its fringe of threads)." Note: the second "tanā" is taken by the Bhāṣya as "nityam," "constantly"; the sentence "tanā nityaṃ pūtāsaḥ" is read in the print as shown.

The Nirukta's etymologies of "Indra." The Bhāṣya now cites Yāska (Nirukta 10-8): Reading note: the clause after "karmaṇa" is printed "ಇಞ್ಛತ್ರೂಣಾಂ" — इञ्छत्रूणां (iñ chatrūṇāṃ, i.e. "in" + "śatrūṇām" in sandhi); re-read from the better scan, Oct 2026. "idanter" is also printed thus, where a form of the root "ind/ind" might be expected. "vera/vendave" etc. are "vā + irām / vā + indave," in sandhi.

इन्द्रशब्दं यास्को बहुधा निर्वक्ति । इन्द्र इरां दृणातीति वेरां ददातीति वेरां दधातीति वेरां दारयतीति वेरां धारयतीति वेन्दवे द्रवतीति वेन्दौ रमत इति वेन्द्धे भूतानीति वा तद्यदेनं प्राणैः समैन्धंस्तदिन्द्रस्येन्द्रत्वमिति विज्ञायत इदंकरणादित्याग्रायण इदं दर्शनादित्यौपमन्यव इदन्तेर्वैश्वर्यकर्मण इञ्छत्रूणां दारयिता वा द्रावयिता वादरयिता च यज्वनाम् । नि. १०-८ । indra-śabdaṃ yāsko bahudhā nirvakti | indra irāṃ dṛṇātīti verāṃ dadātīti verāṃ dadhātīti verāṃ dārayatīti verāṃ dhārayatīti vendave dravatīti vendauramata iti vendhe bhūtānīti vā tad yad enaṃ prāṇaiḥ samaindhaṃs tad indrasyendratvam iti vijñāyata idaṃ-karaṇād ity āgrāyaṇa idaṃ darśanād ity aupamanyava idanter vaiśvarya-karmaṇa iñ chatrūṇāṃ dārayitā vā drāvayitā vādarayitā ca yajvanām | ni. 10-8 |

Translation: "Yāska explains the word 'Indra' in many ways: 'Indra' — either because he tears open ('dṛṇāti') the 'irā' (food/nourishment); or because he gives ('dadāti') irā; or because he holds/supports ('dadhāti') irā; or because he splits ('dārayati') irā; or because he sustains ('dhārayati') irā; or because he runs ('dravati') to the 'indu' (Soma-drop); or because he delights ('ramate') in the Soma-drop; or because he kindles ('indhe') living beings. And it is known (from the Brāhmaṇa) that 'because they kindled him ('samaindhan') with the vital breaths, that is the Indra-hood of Indra.' Āgrāyaṇa says: 'from "idaṃ-karaṇa," making this (world).' Aupamanyava says: 'from "idaṃ-darśana," seeing this.' [The next clause, drawing on the root 'ind' in the sense of lordship, and the closing sense — Indra as the one who tears apart, drives off, and shatters (the foes) and protects the sacrificers — is partly blurred in the print and given here as a paraphrase, not a verified reading.] (Nirukta 10.8)"

इति । अस्यायमर्थः । दृ विदारण इति धातुः । इरामन्नमुद्दिश्य तन्निष्पादकजलसिद्ध्यर्थं दृणाति मेघं विदीर्णं करोतीतीन्द्रः । डुदाञ् दान इति धातुः । इरामन्नं वृष्टिनिष्पादनेन ददातीतीन्द्रः । धाञ् पोषणार्थः । इरामन्नं तृप्तिकारणं सस्यं दधाति जलप्रदानेन पुष्णातीतीन्द्रः । इरामुत्पादयितुं कर्षकमुखेन भूमिं विदारयतीतीन्द्रः । पूर्वोक्तपोषणमुखेनेरां धारयति विनाशराहित्येन स्थापयतीतीन्द्रः । इन्दुः सोमो वल्लीरसः । तदर्थं यागभूमौ द्रवति धावतीतीन्द्रः । इन्दौ यथोक्ते सोमे रमते क्रीडतीतीन्द्रः । ञिइन्धी दीप्ताविति धातुः । भूतानि प्राणिदेहानिन्द्धे जीवचैतन्यरूपेणान्तः प्रविश्य दीपयतीतीन्द्रः । iti | asyāyam arthaḥ | dṛ vidāraṇa iti dhātuḥ | irām annam uddiśya tan-niṣpādaka-jala-siddhy-arthaṃ dṛṇāti megham vidīrṇaṃ karotīti indraḥ | ḍudāñ dāna iti dhātuḥ | irām annaṃ vṛṣṭi-niṣpādanena dadātīti indraḥ | dhāñ poṣaṇārthaḥ | irām annaṃ tṛpti-kāraṇaṃ sasyaṃ dadhāti jala-pradānena puṣṇātīti indraḥ | irām utpādayituṃ karṣaka-mukhena bhūmiṃ vidārayatīti indraḥ | pūrvokta-poṣaṇa-mukhenerāṃ dhārayati vināśa-rāhityena sthāpayatīti indraḥ | induḥ somo vallī-rasaḥ | tad-arthaṃ yāga-bhūmau dravati dhāvatīti indraḥ | indau yathokte some ramate krīḍatīti indraḥ | ñi-indhī dīptāv iti dhātuḥ | bhūtāni prāṇi-dehān indhe jīva-caitanya-rūpeṇāntaḥ praviśya dīpayatīti indraḥ |

Translation: "The sense of this is as follows. (1) The root is 'dṛ,' in the sense of splitting: aiming at irā (food), and for the sake of producing the water that produces it, he splits the cloud open — hence Indra. (2) The root is 'ḍudāñ,' to give: he gives irā, food, by bringing rain about — hence Indra. (3) The root is 'dhāñ,' for nourishing: he supports irā, food — the grain that is the cause of satiety — nourishing it by the gift of water — hence Indra. (4) To bring forth irā he splits the earth, by means of the ploughman — hence Indra. (5) By means of the nourishment mentioned above he sustains irā, he establishes it free from destruction — hence Indra. (6) 'Indu' is the Soma, the juice of the creeper: for its sake he runs, he hastens, to the ground of the sacrifice — hence Indra. (7) He delights, he plays, in the Soma, the 'indu' as described — hence Indra. (8) The root is 'ñi-indhī,' in the sense of kindling: he kindles living beings — the bodies of creatures — by entering within them in the form of life-consciousness — hence Indra."

एतदेवाभिप्रेत्य वाजसनेयिन आमनन्ति । इन्धो ह वै नाम्येष योऽयं दक्षिणेऽक्षन्पुरुषः । तं वा एतमिन्धं सन्तमिन्द्र इत्याचक्षते । परोक्षेण परोक्षप्रिया इव हि देवाः प्रत्यक्षद्विषः शत. ब्रा. १४-६-१०-२ । इति । तद्यदित्यादिकं ब्राह्मणान्तरवाक्यम् । तत्रेन्द्रविषये निर्वचनमुच्यत इति शेषः । etad evābhipretya vājasaneyina āmananti | indho ha vai nāmy eṣa yo'yaṃ dakṣiṇe'kṣan puruṣaḥ | taṃ vā etam indhaṃ santam indra ity ācakṣate | parokṣeṇa parokṣa-priyā iva hi devāḥ pratyakṣa-dviṣaḥ | śata. brā. 14-6-10-2 | iti | tad yad ity ādikaṃ brāhmaṇāntara-vākyam | tatra indra-viṣaye nirvacanam ucyata iti śeṣaḥ |

Translation: "With just this in view the Vājasaneyins (the White-Yajurveda school) declare: '"Indha" indeed is the name of this person who is here in the right eye; and him, though he is "Indha," they call "Indra" — by way of indirect speech; for the gods love the indirect, and are averse to the direct.' (Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 14.6.10.2 [as read in the print]). The sentence beginning 'tad yad…' ('that which…') is from another Brāhmaṇa; the supplied sense is 'in it, an etymology concerning Indra is given.'" Note: "nāmy eṣa" is the print's reading as it could be made out; the sense, 'is the name — this one,' is not affected.

यद्यस्मात्कारणादेनं परमात्मरूपमिन्द्रं देवं प्राणैर्वाक्चक्षुरादीन्द्रियैः प्राणापानादिवायुभिश्च सहितं समैन्धन्नुपासका ध्यानेन सम्यक् प्रकाशितवन्तस्तस्मात्कारणादिन्द्रनाम संपन्नम् — अस्मिन्पक्ष इध्यते दीप्यत इति कर्मणि व्युत्पत्तिः । आग्रायणनामको मुनिरिदंकरणादिन्द्र इति निर्वचनं मन्यते । इन्द्रो हि परमात्मरूपेणेदं जगत्करोति । औपमन्यवनामको मुनिरिदंदर्शनादिन्द्र इति निर्वचनमाह । इदमित्यापरोक्ष्यमुच्यते । विवेकेन हि परमात्मानमापरोक्ष्येण पश्यति । एतदेवाभिप्रेत्यारण्यककाण्डे समाम्नायते स एतमेव पुरुषं ब्रह्म ततमम् अपश्यदिदमदर्शमिती३ । तस्मादिदन्द्रो नामेदन्द्रो ह वै नाम तमिदन्द्रं सन्तमिन्द्र इत्याचक्षते परोक्षेण परोक्षप्रिया इव हि देवाः ऐ. आ. २-४-३ । इति । इदि परमैश्वर्य इति धातुः । स्वमायया जगद्रूपत्वं परमैश्वर्यम् । तद्योगादिन्द्रः । अनेनाभिप्रायेण श्रूयते । इन्द्रो… yad yasmāt kāraṇād enaṃ paramātma-rūpam indraṃ devaṃ prāṇair vāk-cakṣur-ādīndriyaiḥ prāṇāpānādi-vāyubhiś ca sahitaṃ samaindhann upāsakā dhyānena samyak prakāśitavantas tasmāt kāraṇād indra-nāma sampannam — asmin pakṣa idhyate dīpyata iti karmaṇi vyutpattiḥ | āgrāyaṇa-nāmako munir idaṃ-karaṇād indra iti nirvacanaṃ manyate | indro hi paramātma-rūpeṇedaṃ jagat karoti | aupamanyava-nāmako munir idaṃ-darśanād indra iti nirvacanam āha | idam ity āparokṣyam ucyate | vivekena hi paramātmānam āparokṣyeṇa paśyati | etad evābhipretyāraṇyaka-kāṇḍe samāmnāyate sa etam eva puruṣaṃ brahma tatamam apaśyad idam adarśam itī3 | tasmād idandro nāmedandro ha vai nāma tam idandraṃ santam indra ity ācakṣate parokṣeṇa parokṣa-priyā iva hi devāḥ | ai. ā. 2-4-3 | iti | idi paramaiśvarya iti dhātuḥ | sva-māyayā jagad-rūpatvaṃ paramaiśvaryam | tad-yogād indraḥ | anenābhiprāyeṇa śrūyate | indro…

Translation: "'Because the worshippers, by meditation, fully kindled this god Indra — whose form is the Supreme Self — together with the senses (vital breaths, speech, sight and the rest) and the vital airs (prāṇa, apāna and the rest), therefore the name "Indra" arose' — in this view ('asmin pakṣe') the derivation is in the passive: 'he is kindled, shines.' The sage named Āgrāyaṇa holds the etymology 'Indra, from idaṃ-karaṇa (making this)'; for Indra, in the form of the Supreme Self, makes this world. The sage named Aupamanyava gives the etymology 'Indra, from idaṃ-darśana (seeing this)'; 'idam' (this) here denotes direct, immediate vision — for through discrimination one sees the Supreme Self directly. With exactly this in view it is recited in the Āraṇyaka section: 'He beheld this very Person, Brahman, the all-pervading [?]: "I have seen this!" (— and so on). Therefore he is "Idandra" by name; "Idandra" indeed is his name; and him, though he is "Idandra," they call "Indra" — by indirect speech; for the gods love the indirect' (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 2.4.3 [as read in the print]). The root 'idi' means 'supreme lordship'; the supreme lordship is the becoming-the-world of him by his own māyā; by connection with this he is Indra. With this intention it is heard: 'Indra…'" continues on the next page Page header: "Mandala 1, Anuvāka 1, Sūkta 3." Continuing from the previous page, where the Bhāṣya was quoting "indro…".

original p. 32

Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya concluded; Pada-meanings; Bhāvārtha; English rendering

इन्द्रो मायाभिः पुरुरूप ईयते ऋग्वे. ६-४७-१८ । इति इनशब्दस्येश्वरवाचकस्याकारलोपे सति नकारान्तमिन्निति पदं भवति । द्वा [sic: दृ ?] भये इति धातुः । स च परमेश्वरः शत्रूणां दारयित्वा भीषयितेतीन्द्रः । द्रु गताविति धातुः । शत्रूणां द्रावयित्वा पलायनं प्रापयितेतीन्द्रः । यज्वनां योगानुष्ठायिनामादरयिता भयस्य परिहर्ता । एवमेतानि निर्वचनानि द्रष्टव्यानीति । indro māyābhiḥ pururūpa īyate | ṛgve. 6-47-18 | iti ina-śabdasyeśvara-vācakasyākāra-lope sati nakārāntam in iti padaṃ bhavati | dvā [sic: dṛ ?] bhaye iti dhātuḥ | sa ca parameśvaraḥ śatrūṇāṃ dārayitvā bhīṣayitety indraḥ | dru gatāv iti dhātuḥ | śatrūṇāṃ drāvayitvā palāyanaṃ prāpayitety indraḥ | yajvanāṃ yogānuṣṭhāyinām ādarayitā bhayasya parihartā | evam etāni nirvacanāni draṣṭavyānīti |

Translation: "'Indra goes forth in many forms by his māyās' (Ṛgveda 6.47.18). Here the word 'ina,' denoting the Lord, on losing its 'a' becomes the word 'in,' ending in n. (9) The root is 'dvā [sic; the root meant is probably dṛ]' in the sense of fear: that Supreme Lord, tearing the enemies apart, frightens them — hence Indra. (10) The root is 'dru,' in the sense of going: he makes the enemies run, brings them to flight — hence Indra. (11) He is the honourer of the sacrificers who practise yoga, and the one who carries them across fear. In this way these etymologies are to be understood." Reading notes: the Ṛgveda reference is read from the print as "6-47-18"; the print's root-name before "bhaye" is unclear — "dṛ" is the best reading, and the sense is not affected.

॥ Vyākaraṇa notes within the Bhāṣya ॥ short; transcribed in full

इन्द्रेत्यत्रामन्त्रिताद्युदात्तत्वम् । आ इत्यत्र निपातत्वेनाद्युदात्तः । चित्रभानो । पदात्परत्वादामन्त्रितनिघातः । त्वामिच्छन्तीत्यर्थे युष्मच्छब्दात्सुप आत्मनः क्यच् । पा. सू. ३-१-८ । प्रत्ययोत्तरपदयोश्च । पा. ७-२-९८ । इति मपर्यन्तस्य त्वादेशः । क्याच्छन्दसि । पा. ३-२-१७० । इति क्यजन्तादुप्रत्ययः । त्वत्य इति प्राप्ते युष्मदस्मदोरनादेशे पा. ७-२-८६ । इत्यविभक्तावपि हलादौ व्यत्ययेनात्त्वम् । उकारः प्रत्ययस्वरेणाद्युदात्तः । अणुशब्दः सौक्ष्म्यवाचकस्तद्योगात्प्रकृतेऽङ्गुलीषु वर्तते । वोतो गुणवचनात् । पा. ४-१-४४ । इति ङीषि प्राप्ते व्यत्ययेन ङीन् । नित्त्वादाद्युदात्तः । तना इत्ययं निपातो नित्यमित्यर्थे निपातत्वादाद्युदात्तः । पूतासः । आज्जसेरसुक् । पा. ७-१-५० । इत्यसुक् । indretyatrāmantritādyudāttatvam | ā ity atra nipātatvenādyudāttaḥ | citrabhāno | padāt paratvād āmantrita-nighātaḥ | tvām icchantīty arthe yuṣmac-chabdāt sup ātmanaḥ kyac | pā. sū. 3-1-8 | pratyayottarapadayoś ca | pā. 7-2-98 | iti ma-paryantasya tvādeśaḥ | kyāc chandasi | pā. 3-2-170 | iti kyajantād u-pratyayaḥ | tvatya iti prāpte yuṣmadasmador anādeśe pā. 7-2-86 | ity avibhaktāv api halādau vyatyayenātvam | ukāraḥ pratyaya-svareṇādyudāttaḥ | aṇu-śabdaḥ saukṣmya-vācakas tad-yogāt prakṛte 'ṅgulīṣu vartate | voto guṇavacanāt | pā. 4-1-44 | iti ṅīṣi prāpte vyatyayena ṅīn | nittvād ādyudāttaḥ | tanā ity ayaṃ nipāto nityam ity arthe nipātatvād ādyudāttaḥ | pūtāsaḥ | āj-jaser asuk | pā. 7-1-50 | ity asuk |

Translation: "In 'indra' (here a vocative) the first syllable is acute by the vocative rule. 'Ā' is a particle (nipāta), hence acute on its first syllable. 'Citrabhāno' — because it follows another word, the vocative loses its accent (nighāta). 'Tvāyavaḥ' — in the sense 'those who desire you': from the word 'yuṣmad,' the affix 'kyac' after a 'sup'-ending word in the sense of 'one's own wish' (Pāṇini 3.1.8); the substitute 'tva' replaces the stem up to its 'm' (Pāṇini 7.2.98 'pratyayottarapadayoś ca'); then, by 'kyāc chandasi' (Pāṇini 3.2.170), the affix 'u' after a word ending in 'kyac'; where 'tvatya…' would be obtained, the 'a'-substitution takes place by vyatyaya (Vedic licence) even before a non-case-affix beginning with a consonant, per Pā. 7.2.86. The 'u' is acute by the accent of the affix. — 'Aṇvī': the word 'aṇu' denotes fineness; through that association it is applied to the fingers in the present context. Where, by Pā. 4.1.44 ("vāto guṇavacanāt"), the feminine affix ṅīṣ would be expected, 'ṅīn' appears by vyatyaya; since it carries the mark 'n,' the first syllable is acute. 'Tanā' is a particle with the sense 'constantly'; being a particle, first-syllable acute. 'Pūtāsaḥ' — the augment 'asuk' after the 'jas' ending, by Pā. 7.1.50 ('ājjaser asuk')." Reading note, revised at p. 38: at first the opening of this sūtra was read as "voko"; the clearer larger print on p. 38 reads "voto guṇavacanāt" (Pā. 4-1-44), and the text above has been changed to that.

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥ Kannada, translated

चित्रभानो (citrabhāno) — O Indra, who shine with a wonderful, marvellous radiance | आ याहि (ā yāhi) — come (to this sacrificial altar which we are performing) | त्वायवः (tvāyavaḥ) — that which you desire (or: which is dear to you) | इमे सुताः (ime sutāḥ) — these Soma-juices (those extracted by crushing the Soma creeper) | अण्वीभिः (aṇvībhiḥ) — by the fingers (of the priests) (or: by the cloth called the "daśā-pavitra," with which Soma-juice is filtered) | तना (tanā) — always | पूतासः (pūtāsaḥ) — having been purified, are fit to be drunk.

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

O Indra, who shine with wondrous splendour! The priests have prepared the Soma-juice that is dear to you (or, "for your sake") — filtering it well with their fingers (or with a cloth like a fine net), so that it is fit for drinking. To drink that Soma-juice, may you come to this sacrificial altar of ours.

English Translation (printed in English in the source itself):

"Come hither, O Indra, of wonderful splendour; these libations of soma juice, ever pure, expressed by the fingers of the priests are deserious [sic — the source's own misprint, evidently for 'desirous'] of you."

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥

This Rik and the following two are an "aindra-stṛcaḥ" — that is, a tṛca (triplet) related to Indra: three mantras that praise Indra. Page header: "Aṣṭaka 1, Adhyāya 1, Varga 5 · Ṛgveda-saṃhitā." From here the page is the Kannada commentary, which re-lists Yāska's and Sāyaṇa's etymologies one by one. The Sanskrit lemmas it quotes repeat what was already transcribed on pp. 31–32 and are given here in short form, in all three layers.

original p. 33

Kannada commentary: the etymologies of "Indra" (opening)

इन्द्र (indra) — The Bhāṣyakāra, when explaining the derivation of the word "Indra," cites Yāska's Nirukta: "इन्द्र इरां दृणातीति वेरां ददातीति वेरां दधातीति वेरां दारयतीति वेरां धारयतीति वेन्दवे द्रवतीति वेन्दौ रमत इति वेन्द्धे भूतानीति वा तद्यदेनं प्राणैः समैन्धंस्तदिन्द्रस्येन्द्रत्वमिति विज्ञायत इदंकरणादित्याग्रायण इदं दर्शनादित्यौपमन्यव इन्देर्वैश्वर्यकर्मण इभ्रूत्रूणां [?] दारयिता वा द्रावयिता वादरयिता च यज्वनाम् । इति ॥ नि. १०-८ ॥" indra irāṃ dṛṇātīti verāṃ dadātīti verāṃ dadhātīti verāṃ dārayatīti verāṃ dhārayatīti vendave dravatīti vendau ramata iti vendhe bhūtānīti vā tad yad enaṃ prāṇaiḥ samaindhaṃs tad indrasyendratvam iti vijñāyata idaṃ-karaṇād ity āgrāyaṇa idaṃ darśanād ity aupamanyava inder vaiśvarya-karmaṇa ibhrūtrūṇāṃ [?] dārayitā vā drāvayitā vādarayitā ca yajvanām | iti || ni. 10-8 || — The commentator himself then gives the sense of this, as follows. Reading note: the same unclear stretch — "…karmaṇa ibhrū-trūṇāṃ…" — appears here as on p. 31, in slightly different letter-forms. Since it recurs in both places, it looks like a printing/ligature problem in the source rather than a one-off blur; It is left flagged and unrestored.

  1. "dṛ vidāraṇe iti dhātuḥ | irām annam uddiśya tan-niṣpādaka-jala-siddhy-arthaṃ dṛṇāti megham vidīrṇaṃ karotīti indraḥ" (दृ विदारण इति धातुः । इरामन्नमुद्दिश्य तन्निष्पादकजलसिद्ध्यर्थं दृणाति मेघं विदीर्णं करोतीतीन्द्रः) — The root "dṛ" means to tear, to cut. "Irā" means food (āhāra); we obtain it from plants and trees — that is, from the plant kingdom. For that plant kingdom to grow, water is necessary. For the sake of that water — that is, for rain to fall — he cuts open the cloud (with lightning, the thunderbolt-weapon). Because he does so, the name "Indra" arose.

  2. "ḍudāñ dāna iti dhātuḥ | irām annaṃ vṛṣṭi-niṣpādanena dadātīti indraḥ" (डुदाञ् दान इति धातुः । इरामन्नं वृष्टिनिष्पादनेन ददातीतीन्द्रः) — The root "dā" means to give. "Irā" means food. Because he gives food by means of rain, he is called Indra.

  3. "dhāñ poṣaṇārthaḥ | irām annaṃ tṛpti-kāraṇaṃ sasyaṃ dadhāti jala-pradānena puṣṇātīti indraḥ" (धाञ् पोषणार्थः । इरामन्नं तृप्तिकारणं सस्यं दधाति जलप्रदानेन पुष्णातीतीन्द्रः) — The root "dhā" means to nourish. Because he nourishes the crops and the like that yield food, by the gift of water (rain), he is called Indra.

  4. "irām utpādayituṃ karṣaka-mukhena bhūmiṃ vidārayatīti indraḥ" (इरामुत्पादयितुं कर्षकमुखेन भूमिं विदारयतीतीन्द्रः) — For food to be produced, the land must be ploughed. While the land is being ploughed, he makes it split open by the plough and makes it favourable to the crop. Because he does this, he is called Indra.

  5. "pūrvokta-poṣaṇa-mukhenerāṃ dhārayati vināśa-rāhityena sthāpayatīti indraḥ" (पूर्वोक्तपोषणमुखेनेरां धारयति विनाशराहित्येन स्थापयतीतीन्द्रः) — As said before, having nourished the crops and the like, he becomes their protector, so that they do not perish. Because of this, he is called Indra.

  6. "induḥ somo vallī-rasaḥ | tad-arthaṃ yāga-bhūmau dravati dhāvatīti indraḥ" (इन्दुः सोमो वल्लीरसः । तदर्थं यागभूमौ द्रवति धावतीतीन्द्रः) — "Indu" means the Soma-juice prepared from the Soma creeper. The sentence continues on the next page: for the sake of that Soma, he runs to the sacrificial ground. Page header: "Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya-sahitā · Mandala 1, Anuvāka 1, Sūkta 3." Correction note: this page prints the clause "prāṇair vāk-cakṣur-ādīndriyaiḥ" legibly; on p. 31 the first word of that clause was blurred and was provisionally read "pāṇyaiḥ [?]". The p. 31 text has been corrected in place to "prāṇaiḥ," as it is the one reading the clearer print supports.

original p. 34

Kannada commentary: etymologies of "Indra" (continued)

Continuation of (6): … "Having come, hastening — running swiftly — to such a place, for the sake of drinking the Soma, he is called Indra."

  1. "indau yathokte some ramate krīḍatīti indraḥ" (इन्दौ यथोक्ते सोमे रमते क्रीडतीतीन्द्रः) — Because he, satisfied by the Soma-juice just described, disports himself in delight, he is called Indra.

  2. "ñi-indhī dīptāv iti dhātuḥ | bhūtāni prāṇi-dehān indhe jīva-caitanya-rūpeṇāntaḥ praviśya dīpayatīti indraḥ" (ञिइन्धी दीप्ताविति धातुः । भूतानि प्राणिदेहानिन्द्धे जीवचैतन्यरूपेणान्तः प्रविश्य दीपयतीतीन्द्रः) — The root "indh" means to shine, to illumine. Entering the bodies of living beings in the form of consciousness (caitanya), and impelling them to do each of their own deeds, he shines within them; hence he is called Indra.

  3. "yad yasmāt kāraṇād enaṃ paramātma-rūpam indraṃ devaṃ prāṇair vāk-cakṣur-ādīndriyaiḥ prāṇāpānādi-vāyubhiś ca sahitaṃ samaindhann upāsakā dhyānena samyak prakāśitavantas tasmāt kāraṇād indra-nāma sampannam" (यद्यस्मात्कारणादेनं परमात्मरूपमिन्द्रं देवं प्राणैर्वाक्चक्षुरादीन्द्रियैः प्राणापानादिवायुभिश्च सहितं समैन्धन्नुपासका ध्यानेन सम्यक्प्रकाशितवन्तस्तस्मात्कारणादिन्द्रनाम संपन्नम्) — Because worshippers, in meditation, bring this god — whose form is the Supreme Self — to shine forth well, as joined with the vital breaths, with the senses of speech, sight and the rest, and with the vital airs prāṇa, apāna and the rest, the name "Indra" came about.

  4. "āgrāyaṇa-nāmako munir idaṃ-karaṇād indra iti nirvacanaṃ manyate | indro hi paramātma-rūpeṇedaṃ jagat karoti" (आग्रायणनामको मुनिरिदंकरणादिन्द्र इति निर्वचनं मन्यते । इन्द्रो हि परमात्मरूपेणेदं जगत्करोति) — "Idaṃ-karaṇa" ("making this") means: in the form of the Supreme Self, Indra creates (brings forth) this world; and so, says the sage named Āgrāyaṇa, this god received the name Indra.

  5. "aupamanyava-nāmako munir idaṃ-darśanād indra iti nirvacanam āha | idam ity āparokṣyam ucyate" (औपमन्यवनामको मुनिरिदंदर्शनादिन्द्र इति निर्वचनमाह । इदमित्यापरोक्ष्यमुच्यते) — The sage named Aupamanyava says that, because he sees "idam" — that is, everything — the name Indra came about. Here "idam" means "āparokṣya": what is directly present, plain before the eyes (pratyakṣa), as opposed to hidden. The commentary adds: it is precisely for this reason that the Śruti says "parokṣa-priyā iva hi devāḥ" (परोक्षप्रिया इव हि देवाः — "the gods are fond of the indirect, as it were").

  6. "idi paramaiśvarya iti dhātuḥ | sva-māyayā jagad-rūpatvaṃ paramaiśvaryam | tad-yogād indraḥ" (इदि परमैश्वर्य इति धातुः । स्वमायया जगद्रूपत्वं परमैश्वर्यं । तद्योगादिन्द्रः) — The root "idi" carries the sense "supreme lordship." This god, through his own māyā, has the supreme lordship of taking the form of the world… Correction note: on p. 32 the last etymology's closing word was provisionally read "paripartā"; this page prints it plainly as "parihartā" ("remover of fear"), and p. 32 has been corrected in place.

original p. 35

Etymologies of "Indra" concluded; the word "citrabhānu" begins

Continuation of (12): … "…which is the supreme lordship; hence this god is named Indra. This sense is supported by the Vedic sentence 'indro māyābhiḥ pururūpa īyate' (इन्द्रो मायाभिः पुरुरूप ईयते — 'Indra goes about in many forms by his māyās,' Ṛg. Saṃ. 6-47-18)."

  1. "ina-śabdasyeśvara-vācakasyākāra-lope sati nakārāntam in iti padaṃ bhavati | dṛ bhaye iti dhātuḥ | sa ca parameśvaraḥ śatrūṇāṃ dārayitā bhīṣayitety indraḥ" (इनशब्दस्येश्वरवाचकस्याकारलोपे सति नकारान्तमिन्निति पदं भवति । दृ भये इति धातुः । स च परमेश्वरः शत्रूणां दारयिता भीषयितेतीन्द्रः) — The word "ina" denotes the Lord. When the "a" following the "n" of this word "ina" is dropped, the form "in" remains. The root read here as "dṛ" means fear. That god, being the Supreme Lord, frightens the enemies; hence his name Indra.

  2. "dru gatāv iti dhātuḥ | śatrūṇāṃ drāvayitā palāyanaṃ prāpayitety indraḥ" (द्रु गताविति धातुः । शत्रूणां द्रावयिता पलायनं प्रापयितेतीन्द्रः) — The root "dru" means going — that is, to go, to run away. This god makes enemies flee; hence he is named Indra.

  3. "yajvanāṃ yogānuṣṭhāyināṃ ādarayitā bhayasya parihartā" (यज्वनां योगानुष्ठायिनामादरयिता भयस्य परिहर्ता) — Because he honours those who worship him with sacrifices and the like (and who practise yoga), and removes their fear, this god is named Indra.

In just this fashion many more etymologies of the word "Indra" may be devised.

चित्रभानो (citrabhāno) — The Bhāṣyakāra, Skandasvāmī, Veṅkaṭamādhava and the Western scholars as well all explain this word as "one who shines with a wondrous (vicitra) or astonishing radiance." There is no notable difference of opinion among them. The word "citrabhānu" is used with reference to the deities Agni, Indra, Savitṛ and the Maruts. The Ṛks containing the word are given below. The source prints these citations without translation. The short English glosses are editorial, based on the Devanagari read from the page; where a letter or a reference-number was not clear in the print it is marked [?].

विभक्तासि चित्रभानो सिन्धोरूर्मा उ पाके आ । (ऋ. सं. १-२७-६) vibhaktāsi citrabhāno sindhor ūrmā u pāke ā | (ṛ. saṃ. 1-27-6) Gloss: "O wondrously radiant one, you are the apportioner (distributor) … like the wave of the river, near at hand." [tentative]

तं त्वा घृतस्नवीमहे चित्रभानो स्वर्दृशम् । (ऋ. सं. ५-२६-२) taṃ tvā ghṛtasnavīmahe citrabhāno svar-dṛśam | (ṛ. saṃ. 5-26-2) Gloss: "Thee, O wondrously radiant one, who seest the heaven (or: art seen in heaven), we, with ghee-streams, entreat." [tentative]

तं त्वा यमो अचिकेच्चित्रभानो दशान्तरुष्यादतिरोचमानम् । (ऋ. सं. १०-५१-३) taṃ tvā yamo acikec citrabhāno daśāntar uṣyād atirocamānam | (ṛ. saṃ. 10-51-3) Gloss: "Thee, O wondrously radiant one — Yama made known (to the gods) … thee who shinest forth exceedingly." [tentative; the middle phrase "daśāntar uṣyāt" is not rendered with confidence]

समनं चिददहश्चित्रभानोऽव व्राधन्तमभिनद्वृधश्चित् । (ऋ. सं. १०-६९-११) samanaṃ cid adahaś citrabhāno 'va vrādhantam abhinad vṛdhaś cit | (ṛ. saṃ. 10-69-11) Gloss: not attempted with confidence — the printed words, as I read them, do not yield a sure sense; I give the text only. [?]

श्रूया अग्निश्चित्रभानुर्हवं मे विश्वाभिर्गीर्भिरमृतो विचेताः । (ऋ. सं. २-१०-२) śrūyā agniś citrabhānur havaṃ me viśvābhir gīrbhir amṛto vicetāḥ | (ṛ. saṃ. 2-10-2) Gloss: "…Agni, the wondrously radiant, immortal, all-discerning, [hearken] to my call, with all my songs." [tentative; the opening word, re-read from the better scan, is śrūyā (श्रूया), "may (Agni) hear"]

चित्रभानुरुषसां भात्यग्रेऽपां गर्भः प्रस्व१ आ विवेश । (ऋ. सं. ७-९-३) citrabhānur uṣasāṃ bhāty agre 'pāṃ garbhaḥ prasva ā viveśa | (ṛ. saṃ. 7-9-3) Gloss: "The wondrously radiant one shines at the head of the dawns; the embryo of the waters, he has entered into the child-bearing [creatures/plants?]." [tentative]

original p. 36

"citrabhānu" citations concluded; word-notes on "sutāḥ," "tvāyavaḥ," "aṇvībhiḥ," "tanā" (opening)

Page header: "Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya-sahitā · Mandala 1, Anuvāka 1, Sūkta 3." The glosses below are editorial; the source prints these citations without translation. [?] marks a letter or reference-number not clearly legible.

चित्रभानुं रोदसी अन्तरुर्वी स्वाहुतं विश्वतः प्रत्यञ्चम् । (ऋ. सं. ७-१२-१) citrabhānuṃ rodasī antar urvī svāhutaṃ viśvataḥ pratyañcam | (ṛ. saṃ. 7-12-1) Gloss: "Agni, the wondrously radiant, within the two wide worlds (heaven and earth), well-oblated, facing in every direction." [tentative]

मन्द्रं होतारमृत्विजं चित्रभानुं विभावसुम् । (ऋ. सं. ८-४४-६) mandraṃ hotāram ṛtvijaṃ citrabhānuṃ vibhāvasum | (ṛ. saṃ. 8-44-6) Gloss: "The gladdening Hotṛ, the priest, the wondrously radiant, the shining-wealthy one." [tentative]

In these Ṛks the word "citrabhānu" praises Agni.

आस्थाद्रथं सविता चित्रभानुः कृष्णा रजांसि तविषीं दधानः । (ऋ. सं. १-३५-४) āsthād rathaṃ savitā citrabhānuḥ kṛṣṇā rajāṃsi taviṣīṃ dadhānaḥ | (ṛ. saṃ. 1-35-4) Gloss: "Savitṛ, wondrously radiant, has mounted his chariot, bearing power over the dark realms."

Here the word is an adjective of the deity Savitṛ.

महिषासो मायिनश्चित्रभानवो गिरयो न स्वतवसो रघुष्यदः । (ऋ. सं. १-६४-२) mahiṣāso māyinaś citrabhānavo girayo na svatavaso raghuṣyadaḥ | (ṛ. saṃ. 1-64-2) Gloss: "Mighty, possessed of māyā, wondrously radiant, like mountains self-strong, swift-gliding."

आ गच्छन्तीमवसा चित्रभानवः कामं विप्रस्य तर्पयन्त धामभिः । (ऋ. सं. १-८५-११) ā gacchantīm avasā citrabhānavaḥ kāmaṃ viprasya tarpayanta dhāmabhiḥ | (ṛ. saṃ. 1-85-11) Gloss: "The wondrously radiant ones, coming with their aid, satisfy the sage's desire with their powers."

Here the word "citrabhānavaḥ" refers to the Marut deities.

सुताः (sutāḥ) — The word "sutāḥ" means "pressed out, extracted." सोमाः (somāḥ) — the words "Soma-juices" must be supplied (adhyāhāra).

त्वायवः (tvāyavaḥ) — This word is the nominative plural and is an adjective of "sutāḥ." Here "tvā" means "yuṣmat" ("your / belonging to you").

अण्वीभिः (aṇvībhiḥ) — This word, which ends in the instrumental plural, is used only in this Ṛk. The print says "caturthī-bahuvacana-anta"— "ending in the dative plural" — but "-bhiḥ" is the instrumental plural; this is evidently a slip in the source and is recorded here, not corrected silently. Among the twenty-two words that denote "aṅguli" (finger), the word "aṇvī" is read (Nighaṇṭu 2-5 [print: "ni. 2-5"]). The Bhāṣyakāra and the others also all explain this word as "fingers." Because the word is derived from "aṇu" (very small, fine), some think that the word means "a cloth with many fine openings — a net — used to strain the Soma." But when the Soma creeper is crushed with the stones (grāvāṇa), fingers must be used in straining it; so to say "aṇvībhiḥ sutāḥ" — "the juice extracted with the fingers" — is right. Moreover, since "pūtāsaḥ" already carries the sense "purified," "purified with fingers" and "purified with a net-like cloth" are equally fitting. This is why some accept the sense "with a net-like cloth" for "aṇvībhiḥ." But because the Nirukta states plainly that "aṇvī" is a word for the fingers, this sense in particular is to be accepted.

तना (tanā) — The Bhāṣyakāra calls this word an indeclinable (avyaya) and gives it the sense "always" (yāvāgalū). Apart from that sense, different senses are given in different places. Skanda[svāmī]… Page header: "Aṣṭaka 1, Adhyāya 1, Varga 5 · Ṛgveda-saṃhitā." The English glosses are editorial; the source gives none for these.

original p. 37

"tanā" (Skandasvāmī and Soma-passages); "pūtāsaḥ"; Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā begins

Continuing the note on "tanā" from p. 36: … Skandasvāmī, when giving the meaning of this word, says:

तनाशब्दो दशापवित्रवचनः । अण्वीभिर्दशापवित्रेण च पूताः । हस्तेन दशापवित्रमादाय पूता इत्यर्थः ॥ tanā-śabdo daśā-pavitra-vacanaḥ | aṇvībhir daśā-pavitreṇa ca pūtāḥ | hastena daśā-pavitram ādāya pūtā ity arthaḥ ||

Translation: "The word 'tanā' denotes the daśā-pavitra (the fringed straining-cloth). (The Soma-juices are) purified both by the fingers and by the daśā-pavitra; the meaning is 'purified by taking the daśā-pavitra in the hand.'"

That is, the word "tanā" has the name "daśā-pavitra" (a cloth like a net, used for straining the Soma). Hence the sentence "aṇvībhis tanā pūtāsaḥ" is said to mean "purified by the fingers taking up the cloth and cleansing [the juice]." This sense alone is apt. Although "tanā" has many possible senses, it is most fitting to take "daśā-pavitra" when the word is used in connection with Soma-juice. On this point we give some examples from the Ninth Maṇḍala, where the usages concern Soma:

वारेण शश्वता तना । (ऋ. सं. ९-१-६) vāreṇa śaśvatā tanā | (ṛ. saṃ. 9-1-6) Gloss: "through the ever-[lasting] sieve (of wool), the 'tanā'."

त्वं सोम विपश्चितं तना पुनान आयुषु । (ऋ. सं. ९-१६-८) tvaṃ soma vipaścitaṃ tanā punāna āyuṣu | (ṛ. saṃ. 9-16-8) Gloss: "You, O Soma, being purified through the 'tanā,' among the (human) tribes, [make] the wise one…" [tentative; the middle of the line is not rendered with confidence]

प्र सुवानो धारया तनेन्दुर्हिन्वानो अर्षति । (ऋ. सं. ९-३४-१) pra suvāno dhārayā tanendur hinvāno arṣati | (ṛ. saṃ. 9-34-1) Gloss: "Pressed, the Soma-drop, being impelled, flows forth in a stream through the 'tanā.'"

सहस्रधारो योत् तना । (ऋ. सं. ९-५२-२) sahasra-dhāro yot tanā | (ṛ. saṃ. 9-52-2) Gloss: not attempted — the word "yot" is doubtful as printed.

आययोस्त्रिंशतं तना सहस्राणि च दद्महे । (ऋ. सं. ९-५८-४) āyayos triṃśataṃ tanā sahasrāṇi ca dadmahe | (ṛ. saṃ. 9-58-4) Gloss: "…thirty… through the 'tanā,' and thousands we give." [tentative; the first word is doubtful]

तना कृण्वन्तो अर्वते । (ऋ. सं. ९-६२-२) tanā kṛṇvanto arvate | (ṛ. saṃ. 9-62-2) Gloss: "making [the juice] by means of the 'tanā' for the swift horse (i.e., Indra's)." [tentative]

जहाति वव्रिं पितुरेति निष्कृतमुपप्रुतं कृणुते निर्णिजं तना । (ऋ. सं. ९-७१-२) jahāti vavriṃ pitur eti niṣkṛtam upaprutaṃ kṛṇute nirṇijaṃ tanā | (ṛ. saṃ. 9-71-2) Gloss: "He leaves his covering, goes to his father's appointed place; having flowed, he makes his (bright) garment through the 'tanā.'" [tentative]

पिबन्ति मित्रो अर्यमा तना पूतस्य वरुणः । (ऋ. सं. ८-९४-३) pibanti mitro aryamā tanā pūtasya varuṇaḥ | (ṛ. saṃ. 8-94-3) Gloss: "Mitra, Aryaman and Varuṇa drink the juice purified through the 'tanā.'"

The reference "8-94-3" is as best it could be read; the verse is cited among the Soma-passages although the number begins with "8," which is flagged rather than altered.

In all of these places it is apt to take the word "tanā" as "daśā-pavitra" — in the source's own English parenthesis, "(a fringed filtering cloth)."

पूतासः (pūtāsaḥ) — "Pūtāsaḥ" is an archaic (prācīna) usage of the nominative plural. This form is found only in this Ṛk, nowhere else. The form "pūtāḥ" (without the "-asaḥ") occurs in these Ṛks: Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-29-10; 9-22-3; 9-101-12; 10-19-2 digits of these four references are not clearly legible. In meaning, there is no difference whatever between the two forms.

॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥

In "indra" the vocative accent — acute on the first syllable — occurs. "Ā" is a nipāta (particle); therefore, by "nipātā ādyudāttāḥ" (Phiṭ-sūtra 80 as printed), it takes acute on its first syllable. "Citrabhāno" being a vocative that stands after another word, takes the eighth-chapter vocative-anudātta (aṣṭamika āmantritānudātta). When one wishes to express "tvām icchati" ("he wants you"), by the rule "supa ātmanaḥ kyac" (Pā. Sū. 3-1-8) … continues on the next page; this is the Kannada rendering of the grammar already transcribed in Sanskrit on p. 32 Page header: "Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya-sahitā · Mandala 1, Anuvāka 1, Sūkta 3." This is the Kannada rendering of the grammar already given in Sanskrit on p. 32; translated here in full, since it is short.

Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā for Rik 3.4 concluded; Saṃhitā and Pada text of Rik 3.5

Continuing from p. 37: …the "kyac" affix is added to the word "yuṣmad." By "pratyayottarapadayoś ca" (Pā. Sū. 7-2-98) — when an affix, or a following second member of a compound, that conveys unity of sense (ekārtha) follows, then for the stems "yuṣmad" and "asmad," the portion up to "m" (that is, "yuṣm" and "asm") is replaced respectively by "tva" and "ma." So when the "tva" substitution applies, we have "tva + ad + ya"; by "ato guṇe" (Pā. 6-1-97) the latter form ("pararūpa") results, giving "tvadya." Next, by "kyāc chandasi" (Pā. Sū. 3-2-170) — in the Veda, the affix "u" is added after a root that ends in the "kya" affix; when "u" is added the "a" of the "kya" affix is elided, and in the plural one would expect "tvadyavaḥ." But by "yuṣmadasmador anādeśe" (Pā. Sū. 7-2-86), the stems "yuṣmad" and "asmad" that have not undergone substitution take the substitute "ā" when a consonant-beginning affix that is not a case-ending follows; by vyatyaya (Vedic licence), the "ā" substitute comes even where the following affix is not a case-affix, so that one gets "tva + ā + yu," and by lengthening of the homogeneous vowels (savarṇa-dīrgha) and the nominative-plural ending, "tvāyavaḥ." The "u" affix has the first-syllable acute by the affix-accent.

The word "aṇu" conveys "sūkṣma" (fine, subtle). With the sense of fineness in mind, it conveys in this context the sense "finger." Since it is a guṇavācaka (a word of quality), by "vāto guṇavacanāt" (Pā. Sū. 4-1-44) the feminine affix "ṅīṣ" comes optionally after a quality-word ending in "u"; where "ṅīṣ" was due, here by vyatyaya the affix "ṅīn" comes. Since it is "n"-marked, the accent is on the first syllable.

"Tanā": this is a particle (nipāta) in the sense "nitya" (always); being a nipāta, its first syllable is acute.

In "pūtāsaḥ," by "ājjaser asuk" (Pā. Sū. 7-1-50), the "jas" ending that comes after a stem ending in "a" takes the augment "asuk"; with the "asuk" augment we get "pūtāsas," and with "ru"-substitution and visarga, "pūtāsaḥ." ॥४॥ Accent-notation note: in the Kannada print the Saṃhitā and Pada texts carry accent-marks — short vertical strokes above the syllable (svarita, ॑) and short lines beneath it (anudātta, ॒); the udātta is unmarked. In the Oct 2026 pass the Saṃhitā-pāṭha of every Ṛk is given with these marks as read from the better scan (the IAST line puts an acute on the udātta, derived from the marks); the Pada-pāṭha is given without accents. Earlier notes in this volume that say the accent-marks are not reproduced refer to the Pada text.

Sūkta 3, The Fifth Mantra

॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥ Accents read from the better scan. [accent ?]: the print has a further small mark above व of सुताव॑तः, not identified.

इन्द्रा या॑हि धि॒येषि॒तो विप्र॑जूतः सु॒ताव॑तः । [accent ?] उप॒ ब्रह्मा॑णि वा॒घतः॑ ॥५॥

indrā́ yāhi dhiyéṣitó víprajūtaḥ sutā́vataḥ | [accent ?] upa bráhmāṇi vāghátaḥ ||5||

Sūkta 3, Fifth Mantra: Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya, Pada-meanings, Bhāvārtha, English rendering

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥

हे इन्द्र त्वमा याहि । अस्मिन्कर्मण्यागच्छ । किमर्थम् । वाघत ऋत्विजो ब्रह्माणि वेदरूपाणि स्तोत्राण्युपैतुम् । कीदृशस्त्वम् । धियोऽस्मदीयया प्रज्ञयेषितः प्राप्तः । अस्मद्भक्त्या प्रेरित इत्यर्थः । विप्रजूतः । यथा यजमानभक्त्या प्रेरितस्तथान्यैरपि विप्रैर्मेधाविभिरृत्विग्भिः प्रेरितः । कीदृशस्य वाघतः । सुतावतः अभिषुतसोमयुक्तस्य ॥ he indra tvam ā yāhi | asmin karmaṇy āgaccha | kim artham | vāghata ṛtvijo brahmāṇi veda-rūpāṇi stotrāṇy upaitum | kīdṛśas tvam | dhiyo 'smadīyayā prajñayeṣitaḥ prāptaḥ | asmad-bhaktyā prerita ity arthaḥ | viprajūtaḥ | yathā yajamāna-bhaktyā preritas tathānyair api viprair medhāvibhir ṛtvigbhiḥ preritaḥ | kīdṛśasya vāghataḥ | sutāvataḥ abhiṣuta-soma-yuktasya ||

Translation: "O Indra, come here. Come to this rite. For what purpose? To approach the 'brahmāṇi' — the Veda-form praise-hymns — of the Vāghata, the priests. What kind are you? 'Dhiyā iṣitaḥ' — reached (prāptaḥ), moved, by our understanding; that is, impelled by our devotion. 'Viprajūtaḥ' — as you are impelled by the sacrificer's devotion, so you are also impelled by other 'vipras' — wise priests (ṛtvijaḥ). Of what sort of Vāghata? 'Sutāvataḥ' — of one who has Soma pressed out and ready." Reading note: the print before "prajñayā" reads "dhiyo 'smadīyayā" (clear in the second scan; the first reading had an extra syllable). The sense — "by our (priestly) understanding" — agrees with the Kannada Pada-meaning below.

केत इत्यादिष्वेकादशसु प्रज्ञानामसु धीरिति पठितम् । चतुर्विंशतिसंख्याकेषु मेधाविनामसु विप्रो धीर इति पठितम् । भरता इत्यादिष्वष्टस्वृत्विङ्नामसु वाघत इति पठितम् । keta ity ādiṣv ekādaśasu prajñā-nāmasu dhīr iti paṭhitam | catur-viṃśati-saṃkhyākeṣu medhāvi-nāmasu vipro dhīra iti paṭhitam | bharatā ity ādiṣv aṣṭasv ṛtvik-nāmasu vāghata iti paṭhitam |

Translation: "Among the eleven names for 'understanding' beginning with 'keta' (in the Nighaṇṭu), 'dhī' is read. Among the twenty-four names for 'the wise,' 'vipra' and 'dhīra' are read. Among the names of the ṛtvij (priest) beginning with 'bharatāḥ,' 'vāghataḥ' is read." Reading note: the count of the ṛtvij-names after "ādiṣu" is clear in the second scan: "aṣṭasv ṛtvijñāmasu" (the print has "-sv" across the line-break); it is read "aṣṭasu ṛtvik-nāmasu," in the eight names of priests.

॥ Grammar within the Bhāṣya ॥ short; given in full

इषित इत्यत्रैष गताविल्यस्मान्निष्ठायामिडागमः । आगमा अनुदात्ताः । म. ३-१-३-७ । इतीटोऽनुदात्तत्वात्क्तस्वरः शिष्यते । विप्रजूतः । डुवप् बीजतन्तुसंताने इति धातोर्ऋज्रेन्द्राग्रवज्रविप्रेत्यादिना । उ. २-२८ । रन्प्रत्ययान्तो विप्रशब्दो निपातितः । निपातनादुपधाया इकारो लघूपधगुणाभावश्च । नित्त्वादाद्युदात्तः । तैर्जूतः । प्राप्तः । जू इति सौत्रो धातुर्गत्यर्थः । श्र्युकः किति । पा. ७-२-११ । इतीट्प्रतिषेधः । तृतीया कर्मणि । पा. ६-२-४८ । इति पूर्वपदप्रकृतिस्वरत्वम् । सुतावतः । छान्दसं दीर्घत्वम् । मतुपोऽनुदात्तत्वात्क्तप्रत्ययस्वर एव शिष्यते । ब्रह्माणि । नब्विषयस्यानिसन्तस्येत्याद्युदात्तः । वाघच्छब्द ऋत्विङ्नामसु पठितः प्रातिपदिकस्वरः ॥ iṣita ity atra iṣa gatāv ity asmān niṣṭhāyām iḍ-āgamaḥ | āgamā anudāttāḥ | ma. 3-1-3-7 | itīṭo 'nudāttatvāt kta-svaraḥ śiṣyate | viprajūtaḥ | ḍuvap bīja-tantu-saṃtāne iti dhātor ṛjrendrāgra-vajra-viprety ādinā | u. 2-28 | ran-pratyayānto vipra-śabdo nipātitaḥ | nipātanād upadhāyā ikāro laghūpadha-guṇābhāvaś ca | nittvād ādyudāttaḥ | tair jūtaḥ | prāptaḥ | jū iti sautro dhātur gaty-arthaḥ | śryukaḥ kiti | pā. 7-2-11 | itīṭ-pratiṣedhaḥ | tṛtīyā karmaṇi | pā. 6-2-48 | iti pūrva-pada-prakṛti-svaratvam | sutāvataḥ | chāndasaṃ dīrghatvam | matupo 'nudāttatvāt kta-pratyaya-svara eva śiṣyate | brahmāṇi | nab-viṣayasyānisantasyety ādyudāttaḥ | vāghac-chabda ṛtvik-nāmasu paṭhitaḥ prātipadika-svaraḥ ||

Translation: "In 'iṣita,' the root is 'iṣ' (to go): in the niṣṭhā (the 'kta' affix) the augment 'iṭ' comes. Augments are anudātta (unaccented) ('āgamā anudāttāḥ'; the source reference as printed is 'ma. 3-1-3-7'); since the 'iṭ' is thus unaccented, the accent of the 'kta' affix remains. — 'Viprajūtaḥ': from the root 'ḍuvap' (to sow, to spread out threads), by 'ṛjrendrāgra-vajra-vipra-…' (Uṇādi-sūtra 2-28) the word 'vipra' is formed with the affix 'ran' by nipātana (irregular formation); by nipātana the penultimate becomes 'i' and the guṇa of a light penultimate does not occur; because it carries the mark 'n,' the first syllable is acute. 'Jūtaḥ' = 'tair jūtaḥ' — gone to / reached by them. 'Jū' is a sautra root (one drawn from the sūtras), in the sense of 'going'; by 'śryukaḥ kiti' (Pāṇini 7-2-11) the augment 'iṭ' is barred. With the rule 'tṛtīyā karmaṇi' (Pāṇini 6-2-48), the accent of the first member of the compound is retained. — 'Sutāvataḥ': the lengthening is Vedic (chāndasa). As the 'matup' affix is unaccented, only the accent of the 'kta' affix remains. — 'Brahmāṇi': by 'nab-viṣayasyānisantasya' (a Phiṭ-sūtra, the number of which is given on p. 42), acute on the first syllable. — 'Vāghata' is a word read among the priest-names; its accent is that of the bare stem (prātipadika-svara)." Reading notes: (i) the print of the 'ṛjrendrāgra…' Uṇādi list is plain and read as given; (ii) the rule "nab-viṣayasyānisantasya" is hard to read here, but is printed plainly on p. 42, where it is attributed to the Phiṭ-sūtras, not to Pāṇini; "Pā. 6-1-223" had first been written from memory, and that attribution has been withdrawn above; (iii) "vāghata-śabda" is printed "vāghac-chabda"; The word is read as "vāghata."

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥

(हे) इन्द्र (he indra) — O Indra, (you) | धिया (dhiyā) — by our understanding (devotion) | इषितः (iṣitaḥ) — impelled, and | विप्रजूतः (viprajūtaḥ) — impelled also by the wise, intelligent priests | सुतावतः (sutāvataḥ) — of him who has made ready and set by the Soma-juice | वाघतः (vāghataḥ) — of the priest | ब्रह्माणि (brahmāṇi) — the praise-hymns that have the form of the Veda | उप (upa) — in order to approach | आ याहि (ā yāhi) — come (to this rite-of-sacrifice that we are performing).

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

O Indra! We, and the priests too, praise you with devotion. And the priest has prepared the Soma-juice. Impelled by our devotion, to drink it, and also to accept the Veda-form praise-hymns that we chant, may you come to this sacrificial rite that we are performing.

English Translation (printed in English in the source itself):

"O Indra, you are moved by our devoted prayers and that of learned men. Come hither to receive our prayers and the soma juice pressed and prepared for your sake." Special topics on Rik 3.5: "dhiyā," "iṣitaḥ," "viprajūtaḥ"

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥

धिया (dhiyā) — This is the instrumental singular of the word "dhī." The word is read among the eleven names that denote "prajñā" (understanding), beginning with "keta" (in the Nighaṇṭu). Its sense here is "by understanding, by discrimination, by a devotion that is attended by the mind (manaḥ-pūrvaka)." Scholars ancient and modern (Indian and Western) have given this word a variety of senses according to the context; those senses will be discussed in the respective places.

इषितः (iṣitaḥ) — This word is derived from the root "iṣ" (to go). Its sense here is "called, impelled, entreated."

विप्रजूतः (viprajūtaḥ) — A compound made of the two words "vipra" and "jūta." The word "vipra" is read among the twenty-four words that denote "the intelligent." Hence for this word the sense is "the wise, those possessed of understanding, those who have the power of discrimination." "Jūtaḥ" means "prāptaḥ, abhiṣṭutaḥ, preritaḥ" — that is, attained; praised; impelled (corrected from the second scan, which prints "abhiṣṭutaḥ", agreeing with the Kannada gloss "praised"). Although in later (modern) Sanskrit the sense "Brāhmaṇa" is established for "vipra," in Vedic literature — and in the Rigveda in particular — the word is not used in this sense. The word "vipra" is used in many Ṛks of the Rigveda, but "viprajūtaḥ" occurs in this Ṛk alone, nowhere else. For the word "jūtaḥ" the Bhāṣyakāra in many places gives the sense "prāpta" (attained) and "preraṇa" (impelling). For example:

शोचिष्केशं वृषणं यमिमा विशः प्रावन्तु जूतये विशः ॥ (ऋ. सं. १-१२७-२) śociṣkeśaṃ vṛṣaṇaṃ yam imā viśaḥ prāvantu jūtaye viśaḥ || (ṛ. saṃ. 1-127-2) Gloss: "The flame-haired bull, whom these clans, these clans, would favour for [his] speed/impulse."

In this Ṛk, "jūtaye" is also taken to mean "prāptaye" ("for the attaining").

वीळुपत्मभिराशुहेमभिर्वा देवानां वा जूतिभिः शाशदानाः ॥ (ऋ. सं. १-११६-२) vīḷupatmabhir āśuhemabhir vā devānāṃ vā jūtibhiḥ śāśadānāḥ || (ṛ. saṃ. 1-116-2) Gloss: "With (steeds) of firm wings, swift-impelling, or with the impulses of the gods, [you two] being foremost…" [tentative]

In this Ṛk, "jūtibhiḥ" is taken to mean also "preraṇaiḥ" ("by impellings"). Some examples that indicate this sense when "jūta" stands as the latter member of a compound are given below:

अद्रिजूतः — रथो ह वामृतेजा [print: "vāmṛtejā"] अद्रिजूतः परि द्यावापृथिवी याति सद्यः । (ऋ. सं. ३-५८-८) adrijūtaḥ — ratho ha vāmṛtejā [sic] adrijūtaḥ pari dyāvāpṛthivī yāti sadyaḥ | (ṛ. saṃ. 3-58-8) Gloss: "Your chariot, speeded by the (pressing-)stones [adri-jūtaḥ], circles heaven and earth at once."

आदित्यजूतः — दधानो गोमदश्ववत्सुवीर्यमादित्यजूत एधते । (ऋ. सं. ८-४६-५) ādityajūtaḥ — dadhāno gomad aśvavat suvīryam ādityajūta edhate | (ṛ. saṃ. 8-46-5) Gloss: "Bearing wealth in cattle and horses and brave progeny, he who is impelled by the Ādityas prospers."

इन्द्रजूतः — यदङ्ग त्वा भरताः सन्तरेयुर्गव्यन् ग्राम इषित इन्द्रजूतः । (ऋ. सं. ३-३३-११) indrajūtaḥ — yad aṅga tvā bharatāḥ santareyur gavyan grāma iṣita indrajūtaḥ | (ṛ. saṃ. 3-33-11) Gloss: "When, O (river), the Bharatas would cross you, seeking cattle, the host sent forth, impelled by Indra."

The Ṛg-vedic reference-numbers are printed in small Kannada numerals and a number of them are hard to read; every reference that is not certain is marked [?]. Glosses are editorial; the source gives none. The page also contains a block of English printed in the source itself, reproduced as printed.

देवजूतः — महा ऋषिर्देवजा देवजूतोऽस्तभ्नात्सिन्धुमर्णवं नृचक्षाः । (ऋ. सं. ३-५३-९ तथा ४-११-४; ७-८४-३; ८-३१-३) devajūtaḥ — mahā ṛṣir devajā devajūto 'stabhnāt sindhum arṇavaṃ nṛcakṣāḥ | (ṛ. saṃ. 3-53-9 and 4-11-4; 7-84-3; 8-31-3) Gloss: "The great seer, born of the gods, impelled by the gods, a watcher of men, held up the river, the flood."

बाहुजूतः — युष्मादेति मुष्टिहा बाहुजूतो युष्मत्सदश्वो मरुत सुवीरः । (ऋ. सं. ५-५८-४) bāhujūtaḥ — yuṣmād eti muṣṭihā bāhujūto yuṣmatsadaśvo maruta suvīraḥ | (ṛ. saṃ. 5-58-4) Gloss: "From you, O Maruts, goes the fist-striker, impelled by his arm, the hero blessed with horses, rich in heroes through you."

वातजूतः — वि वातजूतो अतसेषु तिष्ठते वृथा जुहूभिः सृण्या तुविष्वणिः । (ऋ. सं. १-५८-४ तथा १-६५-४; १०-१७-१) vātajūtaḥ — vi vātajūto atasesu tiṣṭhate vṛthā juhūbhiḥ sṛṇyā tuviṣvaṇiḥ | (ṛ. saṃ. 1-58-4 and 1-65-4; 10-17-1) Gloss: "Impelled by the wind, he stands out amid the brush, in vain with tongues, with his sickle-like (flame), loud-sounding."

श्येनजूतः — अप्सु द्रप्सो वावृधे श्येनजूतो दुह ईं पिता दुह ईं पितुर्जाम् । (ऋ. सं. ९-८९-२) śyenajūtaḥ — apsu drapso vāvṛdhe śyenajūto duha īṃ pitā duha īṃ pitur jām | (ṛ. saṃ. 9-89-2) Gloss: "The drop has grown in the waters, impelled by the falcon; the father milks him, he milks the father's kinswoman." [tentative]

On "vipra" (Western renderings). Ludwig, Williams, Griffith and other Western scholars have given the word "vipra," in different Ṛks, such meanings as — the source here prints the list in English — "Sage, wise, skilled in work or rite, skilled in speech, singer, Priest, Worshipper, Sacrificer [print: 'Sacrificier'], Fulfiller, Giver of delight, courageous, Sagacious, Pious, Brahmana," and the like; but they say that for this word in this Ṛk the sense "Prudent or intelligent" (that is, discerning, intelligent) fits.

सुतावतः (sutāvataḥ), or "sutavataḥ" — The word "suta" is a word formed from a root meaning "to press out (the juice)" ("su"). The derivation of "sutāvataḥ" is: "sutaḥ somaḥ asyāsti iti sutāvān, tasya sutāvataḥ" — "he who has the pressed Soma is 'sutāvān'; of him, 'sutāvataḥ'." This word is an adjective of the word "vāghataḥ." The word is commonly used in contexts where the Soma-juice is crushed and extracted.

उप (upa) — near, close; or, going near; attaining proximity, and the like.

ब्रह्माणि (brahmāṇi) — The Bhāṣyakāra explains this word as "stotra" (a hymn of praise). Skandasvāmī — in accordance with the sūtra of the Nighaṇṭu (2-7) — gives for the word "brahma" two senses: "anna" (food) and "stotra." Western scholars — Ludwig, Williams, Griffith and others — give for the word, according to context, the source's English list: "Sacred Word, Prayer [print: 'Preyer'], Stotra [print: 'Strotra'], Homage, honour, song, libation, oblation, Praise, adoration, Devotion, Offering, Sacred rite, Food." Although they use different words, there is no great difference from the senses used by Sāyaṇa and Skandasvāmī.

वाघतः (vāghataḥ) — Because the Nighaṇṭu itself plainly states that this word means "ṛtvik" (priest), the Bhāṣyakāra, Skandasvāmī and the others have approved this sense. The view of the Western scholars is not at odds with this sense either; only the words they use are different. This word is used in the Rigveda in only the following eleven Ṛks: 1-3-5; 1-58-7; 1-88-6; 1-110-4; 3-2-1; 3-37-2; 6-16-13; 7-32-1; 8-78-4; 10-62-7; 3-60-4. All eleven re-read from the better scan, Oct 2026 numeral pass. Page header: "Mandala 1, Anuvāka 1, Sūkta 3." Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā for Rik 3.5 (Kannada); Saṃhitā and Pada text of Rik 3.6

॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥

After the root "iṣ gatau" (iṣa gatau), when the affix "kta" is added, by "ārdhadhātukasyeḍ valādeḥ" (Pā. Sū. 7-2-35) — the augment "iṭ" comes to "ta" — and "iṣitaḥ" results. Here, by "āgamā anudāttāḥ" (Pā. Sū. 3-1-3, vārttika 7) — "augments are unaccented" — the "i" becomes unaccented; hence the accent of the "kta" affix remains.

The root "ḍu vap bīja-saṃtāne": by "ṛjrendrāgra-vajra-vipra-…" (Uṇ. Sū. 2-186 [as printed; on p. 39 the same sūtra is cited as 2-28]), these nineteen words are formed with the affix "ran" by nipātana (irregular formation). The list as printed:

ऋज्रेन्द्राग्रवज्रविप्रकुब्रचुब्रक्षुरखुरभद्रोग्रभेरभेलशुक्रशक्लगौरवन्वेरमालाः ṛjrendrāgra-vajra-vipra-kubra-cubra-kṣura-khura-bhadrogra-bhera-bhela-śukra-śakla-gaurava-nvera-mālāḥ

The division of this list into words is a best reading; "kubra," "cubra," and the last few members are not certain. By the very nipātana, the "a" of the root "vap" becomes "i", and the guṇa of the light penultimate "i" does not occur. Since it is n-marked, the first syllable is acute: "viprajūtaḥ." "Jū" is a sautra root (one given in the sūtras), meaning "gati" (going). To the "kta" affix that follows the root "jū," "iṭ" would come by "ārdhadhātukasyeḍ valādeḥ"; but by "śryukaḥ kiti" (Pā. Sū. 7-2-10 [as printed]) — the root "śri," and the one-syllable roots ending in the vowels "u," "ṛ," [and others (the print's list is unclear)] — no "iṭ" comes before affixes marked "g," "k" ("git," "kit"); so the "iṭ" is prohibited. Then, by "tṛtīyā karmaṇi" (Pā. Sū. 6-2-48) — when a word ending in the "kta" affix, with the sense of the object (karman), follows, a word in the instrumental case retains its natural accent (prakṛti-svara); hence the accent of the first member remains. From the root "su," adding "kta," one gets "suta." Adding "matup" to it gives "sutavataḥ." By Vedic usage, if the previous member is lengthened it becomes "sutāvataḥ." As "matup" is unaccented, the accent of the "kta" affix remains. "Brahmāṇi" — by "nab-viṣayasyānisantasya" (Phiṭ-sūtra 26) it is acute on the first syllable. As for "vāghat" — since Yāska has read it among the "names of priests" (ṛtvij-nāmadheya) in the Nighaṇṭu, it is a bare stem (prātipadika); hence the prātipadika-accent results. ॥५॥ Saṃhitā accents as printed; Pada unaccented — see the note at Rik 3.5.

Sūkta 3, The Sixth Mantra

॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥

इन्द्रा या॑हि॒ तूतु॑जान॒ उप॒ ब्रह्मा॑णि हरिवः । सु॒ते द॑धिष्व न॒श्चनः॑ ॥६॥

indrā́ yāhi tū́tujāna úpa bráhmāṇi harivaḥ | suté dadhiṣva naścánaḥ ||6||

॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥ Page header: "Aṣṭaka 1, Adhyāya 1, Varga 5 · Ṛgveda-saṃhitā." Sanskrit is printed in Kannada script and rendered here into Devanagari/IAST.

इन्द्र । आ । याहि । तूतुजानः । उप । ब्रह्माणि । हरिवः । सुते । दधिष्व । नः । चनः ॥६॥

original p. 43

Sūkta 3, Sixth Mantra: Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya, grammar, Pada-meanings, Bhāvārtha

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥

हरिशब्द इन्द्रसंबन्धिनोरश्वयोर्नामधेयम् । हरी इन्द्रस्य रोहितोऽग्नेरिति तदीयाश्वनामत्वेन पठितत्वात् । हे हरिवः अश्वयुक्तेन्द्र त्वं ब्रह्माण्युपैतुमा याहि । कीदृशस्त्वम् । तूतुजानः त्वरमाणः । आगत्य चास्मिन्सुते सोमाभिषवयुक्ते कर्मणि नोऽस्मदीयं चनोऽन्नं हविर्लक्षणं दधिष्व धारय । स्वीकुर्वित्यर्थः । hari-śabda indra-sambandhinor aśvayor nāmadheyam | harī indrasya rohito 'gner iti tadīyāśva-nāmatvena paṭhitatvāt | he harivaḥ aśvayuktendra tvaṃ brahmāṇy upaitum ā yāhi | kīdṛśas tvam | tūtujānaḥ tvaramāṇaḥ | āgatya cāsmin sute somābhiṣava-yukte karmaṇi no 'smadīyaṃ cano 'nnaṃ havir-lakṣaṇaṃ dadhiṣva dhāraya | svīkurv ity arthaḥ |

Translation: "The word 'hari' is the name of the two horses connected with Indra, since it is read as the name of his (Indra's) horses in 'harī indrasya, rohita agneḥ' ('the two Haris are Indra's, the Rohita is Agni's' — the Nighaṇṭu's list of horse-names). O 'harivaḥ' — O Indra, yoked with horses — come to approach our 'brahmāṇi.' What kind of one are you? 'Tūtujānaḥ' — hastening. And having come, in this 'sute' (this rite attended with the pressing of Soma), hold ('dadhiṣva') — that is, accept ('svīkuru') — our 'canaḥ,' our food, of the nature of the oblation." Reading note: the first letter of "tadīya" is clear in the second scan as "ta": "tadīyāśva-nāmatvena" ("because they are read as horse-names belonging to him").

॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā within the Bhāṣya ॥ — characterized, not transcribed line-by-line, per the standing convention for dense grammatical derivations; the sūtras it cites are listed in full below.

The Bhāṣya's grammar on this page derives: (a) "tūtujānaḥ" (root "tuj"), (b) "harivaḥ" (vocative of "hari-vat"), (c) "dadhiṣva" (root "dhā," imperative, middle), and (d) "canaḥ" (from "cāy"), and discusses the accent of "brahmāṇi" and its effect on the preceding "upa." One sentence in the middle of this block (the one beginning "brahmāṇīty asya harivaḥ…" and running through "…upety ekārasya sannataraḥ") is too garbled in the print for me to give a reliable reading, so I do not transcribe or translate it; what is plain from it is that it is about why the vocative "harivaḥ" and the following word are accented as they are, and about the "sannatara" (lowered-pitch) accent on the syllable of "upa." The sūtras cited are as follows (numbers as printed; the Sanskrit lines are in the print's own wording): A transliteration of each cited sūtra is: "tujer liṭi liṭaḥ kānaj vā" (pā. 3-2-106) | "tujādīnāṃ dīrgho 'bhyāsasya" (pā. 6-1-7) | "abhyastānām ādiḥ" (pā. 6-1-189) | "chandasīraḥ" (pā. 8-2-15) | "sambuddhau vugid-acām" (pā. 7-1-70, as printed) | "saṃyogānta-lope" (pā. 8-2-23) | "nakārasya matuvaso ruḥ sambuddhau chandasi" (pā. 8-3-1) | "thāsaḥ se" (pā. 3-4-80) | "savābhyāṃ vāmau" (pā. 3-4-91) | "chandasy ubhayathā" (pā. 3-4-117) | "śloś ca dvirbhāvaḥ" (pā. 6-1-10) | "āto lopa iṭi ca" (pā. 6-4-64).

  • "tuj-er liṭi liṭaḥ kānaj vā" — तुजेर्लिटि लिटः कानज्वा (पा. ३-२-१०६) — "the substitute 'kānac' for 'liṭ'" → "tūtujānaḥ." The print has "pujer" for "tujer"; "tuj" is read as the root.
  • "tujādīnāṃ dīrgho 'bhyāsasya" — तुजादीनां दीर्घोऽभ्यासस्य (पा. ६-१-७) — the reduplicative syllable is lengthened.
  • "abhyastānām ādiḥ" — अभ्यस्तानामादिः (पा. ६-१-१८९) — first syllable acute.
  • "chandasīraḥ" — छन्दसीरः (पा. ८-२-१५) — "m" of "matup" becomes "v" after a stem ending in "i" ("hari-vat" for "hari-mat").
  • "sambuddhau … ugidacām" — संबुद्धौ … उगिदचाम् (पा. ७-१-७०) — the augment "num" in the vocative; then संयोगान्तलोपे (पा. ८-२-२३) the loss of the final consonant of the cluster, and नकारस्य मतुवसो रुः संबुद्धौ छन्दसि (पा. ८-३-१) — "ru" for the "n" of "matup" in the vocative → "harivaḥ"; the vocative then takes the eighth-chapter "nighāta."
  • "thāsaḥ se" — थासः से (पा. ३-४-८०) — "se" for "thās" in the imperative; सवाभ्यां वामौ (पा. ३-४-९१) — "va" for the "e" → "dadhiṣva"; छन्दस्युभयथा (पा. ३-४-११७) — in the Veda the ending counts both as "sārvadhātuka" and "ārdhadhātuka," so both "śap" (पा. ३-१-६८) with doubling (श्लौ च द्विर्भावः पा. ६-१-१०) and the "iṭ" augment (पा. ७-२-३५) arise; आतो लोप इटि च (पा. ६-४-६४) — the final "ā" of the root is elided.
  • For "canaḥ": "cāyater anne hrasvaś ca" (from "cāy," with shortening, in the sense "food") with an "asun" ending (Uṇādi 4-199, as printed), the "n" augment from the "ca," and the loss of "y."

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥

हरिवः (harivaḥ) — O you who are accompanied by horses (who sit in a chariot yoked to horses) | इन्द्र (indra) — O Indra, (you) | तूतुजानः (tūtujānaḥ) — being swift, being vigilant | ब्रह्माणि (brahmāṇi) — (the) praise-hymns (that we make) | उप (upa) — in order to accept | आ याहि (ā yāhi) — be one who comes | (and having come) सुते (sute) — in this rite, accompanied by the pressing of the Soma — that is, in this Soma-sacrifice that we are performing | नः (naḥ) — our | चनः (canaḥ) — food of the kind that belongs to the oblation | दधिष्व (dadhiṣva) — "hold" — that is, accept.

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

O Indra! Seated in the chariot to which the horses are yoked, come quickly and with vigilance, to accept the praise-hymns that we make, and the food that we offer in this sacrificial rite, in which we are now drawing out the Soma-juice for you.
