अग्नाविष्णू — अग्नाविष्णू सजोषसा (पुरोनुवाक्या) · अग्नाविष्णू महि धाम (याज्या) agnāviṣṇū — agnāviṣṇū sajoṣasā (puronuvākyā) · agnāviṣṇū mahi dhāma (yājyā) सरस्वती — पावकानः सरस्वती (पुरोनुवाक्या) ऋ. सं. १-३-१० · पावीरवीकन्या (याज्या) ऋ. सं. ६-४९-७ sarasvatī — pāvakā naḥ sarasvatī (puronuvākyā) ṛ. saṃ. 1-3-10 · pāvīravī kanyā (yājyā) ṛ. saṃ. 6-49-7 सरस्वान् — पीपिवांसं सरस्वतः (पुरोनुवाक्या) ऋ. सं. ७-९६-६ · दिव्यं सुपर्णं वायसम् (याज्या) ऋ. सं. १-१५४-२ sarasvān — pīpivāṃsaṃ sarasvataḥ (puronuvākyā) ṛ. saṃ. 7-96-6 · divyaṃ suparṇaṃ vāyasam (yājyā) ṛ. saṃ. 1-154-2 Gloss (mine): "Agnā-Viṣṇū: 'Agni and Viṣṇu, of one mind…' / 'Agni and Viṣṇu, the great abode…'; Sarasvatī: 'Our purifier Sarasvatī…' / 'The purifier, the maiden…'; Sarasvān: 'Sarasvān who is full of [waters]…' / 'The divine, fair-winged bird…'." The Anvārambhaṇīyā mantras (concluded); "pāvakā" and its use for different deities

अग्निर्भगी — आसवं सवितुः (पुरोनुवाक्या) ऋ. सं. ८-१०२-६ · स नो राधांस्या भर (याज्या) ऋ. सं. ७-१५-११ agnir-bhagī — āsavaṃ savituḥ (puronuvākyā) ṛ. saṃ. 8-102-6 · sa no rādhāṃsyā bhara (yājyā) ṛ. saṃ. 7-15-11 Gloss: "(Of Savitṛ) the impulsion of Savitṛ…" / "Bring us, then, bounties…" [tentative; only opening words are given]

That is: in this Anvārambhaṇīyeṣṭi, when the goddess Sarasvatī is invoked, the Ṛk

पावकानः सरस्वती वाजेभिर्वाजिनीवती । यज्ञं वष्टु धियावसुः ॥ (ऋ. सं. १-३-१०) pāvakā naḥ sarasvatī vājebhir vājinīvatī | yajñaṃ vaṣṭu dhiyāvasuḥ || (ṛ. saṃ. 1-3-10) (= the present Rik 3.10; translated above.)

is to be used as the puronuvākyā mantra, and the Ṛk

पावीरवी कन्या चित्रायुः सरस्वती वीरपत्नी धियं धात् । ग्नाभिरच्छिद्रं शरणं सजोषा दुराधर्षं गृणते शर्म यंसत् ॥ (ऋ. सं. ६-४९-७) pāvīravī kanyā citrāyuḥ sarasvatī vīrapatnī dhiyaṃ dhāt | gnābhir acchidraṃ śaraṇaṃ sajoṣā durādharṣaṃ gṛṇate śarma yaṃsat || (ṛ. saṃ. 6-49-7) Gloss (mine): "May Sarasvatī, the maiden, of wondrous life, the hero's consort, grant insight; may she, in concert with the goddess-wives, grant to the singer a shelter without a gap, hard to assail." [tentative]

is to be used as the yājyā mantra — so it is said.

पावका (pāvakā) — This word is derived from the root "pūñ" ("to purify, to cleanse"). The Bhāṣyakāra gives its derivation as "pavanaṃ pāvaḥ śuddhiḥ, taṃ kāyatīti pāvakā" (पवनं पावः शुद्धिस्तं कायतीति पावका — "'pāva' is purification; she who 'makes' that is 'pāvakā'"), i.e., one who purifies; one who cleanses, removing sins. Though the word "pāvaka" is used in many places of deities such as Agni, the Maruts and Soma, it is used especially of Agni: Page header: "Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya-sahitā · Maṇḍala 1, Anuvāka 1, Sūkta 3." Reference-numbers in the five lists below re-read from the better scan, Oct 2026 numeral pass. English words are as printed in the source.

Agni — अग्ने पावक रोचिषा मन्द्रया देव जिह्वया । (ऋ. सं. ५-२६-१) agne pāvaka rociṣā mandrayā deva jihvayā | (ṛ. saṃ. 5-26-1) Gloss: "O purifying Agni, with your light, with your joyful tongue, O god."

स नः पावक दीदिवोऽग्ने देवाँ इहावह । (ऋ. सं. १-१२-१०) sa naḥ pāvaka dīdivo 'gne devāṁ ihāvaha | (ṛ. saṃ. 1-12-10) Gloss: "O shining purifier, bring the gods here."

अस्या जरासो दमा मरित्रा अर्चद्धूमासो अग्नयः पावकाः ॥ (ऋ. सं. १०-४६-७) asyā jarāso damā maritrā arcaddhūmāso agnayaḥ pāvakāḥ || (ṛ. saṃ. 10-46-7) Gloss: "…the purifying fires, with smoke…" [tentative; the first half is not clear to me]

Indra — मिहः पावकाः प्रतता अभूवन्त्स्वस्ति नः पिपृहि पारमासाम् । (ऋ. सं. ३-३१-२०) mihaḥ pāvakāḥ pratatā abhūvan svasti naḥ pipṛhi pāram āsām | (ṛ. saṃ. 3-31-20) Gloss: "The purifying showers have spread out; carry us safely across them."

Uṣas — व्यू व्रजस्य तमसो द्वारोच्छन्तीरव्रञ्छुचयः पावकाः ॥ (ऋ. सं. ४-५१-२) vy ū vrajasya tamaso dvāroc chantīr avran śucayaḥ pāvakāḥ || (ṛ. saṃ. 4-51-2) Gloss: "Shining, they have opened the doors of the dark pen — the bright, purifying (dawns)." [tentative]

original p. 68

"pāvakā" (concluded); "sarasvatī" — the five senses of the word (opening)

In these and other mantras, the word "pāvaka" is used of different deities. Western scholars have explained this word with such words as : "Purifier, purifying, bright, glittering, pure, sacred, blazing, flaming." In the sense relating to Agni, both senses — "that which purifies" and "that which shines" — may be said.

सरस्वती (sarasvatī) — Sāyaṇācārya has given a five-fold account of the sense of the word "sarasvatī" as used in the Ṛgveda mantras:

  1. Nadī (a river) — Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-142-9; 1-164-52; 2-30-8.
  2. The name of a river — Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-3-12; 2-41-16; 3-23-4; 6-61 (the 4th, 7th, 10th, 11th and 13th Ṛks of it); 6-52-6; 6-61-2; 7-36-6; 7-95-1 and 2; 7-96-1; 8-21-17 and 18; 10-64-9; 10-65-13.
  3. The name of a deity — Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-43-11; 5-46-2; 6-49-7; 5-50-12; 10-17-7; 10-30-12.
  4. An ākāśābhimāni-devatā (a deity presiding over the sky-region) — "(one of the three goddesses Iḷā, Bhāratī and Sarasvatī)" — Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-188-8.
  5. Vāgdevī (the goddess of Speech) — Ṛ. Saṃ. 2-1-11; 3-4-8; 3-54-13; 5-42-12; 7-39-5; 7-40-3; 9-67-32.

In the Ṛgveda there are many mantras praising the goddess Sarasvatī. But on the question "who is this goddess Sarasvatī, and what is her nature?" the author of the Nirukta (Yāska) has said nothing; he has said only: "nadīvad devatāvac ca nigamā bhavanti" (नदीवद्देवतावच्च निगमा भवन्ति — nadīvad devatāvac ca nigamā bhavanti — "there are Vedic passages (that treat her) as a river and as a deity"). That is: in some mantras that have the deity Sarasvatī as their subject she is described as a river, and in some as a deity. But it is not clear whether the river named Sarasvatī is regarded as a goddess and praised, or the goddess is regarded as a river and praised. Therefore it must be said that "Sarasvatī" points to both river and deity. In the view that Sarasvatī is a deity, the questions — who is that deity? what is her nature? what are her station and abodes? — cannot easily be answered with a fitting reply. In the view that Sarasvatī is a river, it may be said that a river of that famous name existed in ancient times (the source adds in English: "the modern Sarsuti") and that this very river is praised in the Ṛgveda. When it is said so, a doubt arises: in the sacrifices and the like performed for the sake of particular deities, would not the praise of inanimate things such as rivers be forbidden? … Page header: "Aṣṭaka 1, Adhyāya 1, Varga 6 · Ṛgveda-saṃhitā." Reference-numbers in small Kannada numerals marked [?] where uncertain.

original p. 69

Sarasvatī as river and as deity: the Mīmāṃsā question; five views of the goddess

Continuing from p. 68, at the doubt whether praise of inanimate things like rivers would be forbidden in sacrifices: …"That doubt can be answered. On this point the sage Jaimini, in his Mīmāṃsā-sūtra, raised the objection ("pūrvapakṣa") on the basis of "acetane 'rtha-bandhanāt" (अचेतनेऽर्थबन्धनात् — acetane 'rtha-bandhanāt, जै. सू. १-२-३५) — that is, that where mantras address inanimate things, the connection of sense is [impossible]. To this the Bhāṣyakāra (the Vedāntic commentator) has given the answer by citing the Vedānta-sūtra "abhimāni-vyapadeśaḥ" (अभिमानिव्यपदेशः — abhimāni-vyapadeśaḥ, वे. सू. २-१-५): that is, wherever, in Veda-mantras, inanimate things are addressed, it is to be understood that what is said is addressed to the presiding deities ("abhimāni-devatā") of those inanimate things. (See Part 1, pp. 380–381.) Hence, where a river is praised, it is to be understood that its presiding deity is praised. Concerning this goddess Sarasvatī many persons hold many different views:

  1. In the Purāṇas and elsewhere, "Sarasvatī" means "vāg-adhiṣṭhātrī, śāradā, vidyā-svarūpiṇī, haṃsa-vāhinī" (वागधिष्ठात्री शारदा विद्यास्वरूपिणी हंसवाहिनी) — a particular deity: the presiding deity of speech, famous by the name Śāradā, embodying learning, seated on a swan.
  2. Or: this goddess Sarasvatī is the Āditya (the Sun) specially qualified by a limiting condition ("upādhi"); "upādhi" here means the twilight. So some hold that the Sun, shining at twilight, is here praised in the form of Sarasvatī.
  3. The word "saras" comes from the root "sṛ" (to move, to flow): "saro 'syā asti" or "sarastejo yasyā vidyate sā sarasvatī" — she who has "saras" (radiance, fluid motion) — she who shines in the form of radiance is therefore called "Sarasvatī."
  4. Or (the source quotes Sanskrit here):

अथवा — प्रातर्वाचां प्रवर्तिका, प्राणिनां स्वापपरित्यागेन स्वोचितव्यवहारेषु प्रवृत्तौ शब्दायमानतायाः प्रवृत्तेः, रात्रौ च वाचां निरोधिका रात्रौ प्राणिनां निलायनिलीनत्वेन सुप्यमानतया शब्दविरामात् । एवं च शब्दस्य प्रवर्तिका निवर्तिका एषैव लोके सरस्वतीत्वेन व्यपदिश्यते नान्या ॥ athavā — prātar vācāṃ pravartikā, prāṇināṃ svāpa-parityāgena svocita-vyavahāreṣu pravṛttau śabdāyamānatāyāḥ pravṛtteḥ, rātrau ca vācāṃ nirodhikā rātrau prāṇināṃ nilāya-nilīnatvena supyamānatayā śabda-virāmāt | evaṃ ca śabdasya pravartikā nivartikā eṣaiva loke sarasvatītvena vyapadiśyate nānyā ||

(Reading note: re-read from the better scan, Oct 2026: "svocita" ("their own proper") and "supyamānatayā" ("being asleep").)

Translation of the clear parts, with the Kannada gloss that follows it: "Or: she is the prompter of speech in the morning … and at night the restrainer of speech … and thus, as both the prompter and the stopper of sound, she alone is in the world called Sarasvatī and no other." The Kannada explains: "In the morning the creatures, rising from sleep, set about talking and about their several affairs and activities; at night, the creatures are overcome by sleep, and so, apart from talking and making sounds, they come to rest from their activities and dealings. Therefore, because she is the cause of beginning and ending in the matter of talking or making sound, this goddess of speech is called Sarasvatī."

original p. 70

Sarasvatī: the fifth view (Uṣas); the three questions to be considered; Sarasvatī in Rik 3.10–12; the ṛṣis

  1. As stated before, since the powers of speech and the like belong to this deity, this goddess Sarasvatī is in the form of Uṣas (Dawn). For this very reason, among the words that are the names of the goddess Uṣas — sūnṛtā, sūnṛtāvatī, sūnṛtāvarī and others — the name of this goddess Sarasvatī occurs. Here the word "sūnṛta" means words that are both pleasant and true.

In just this way, in the question of the goddess Sarasvatī, Śaunaka, the author of the Bṛhaddevatā, and other authors have explained her in various ways.

Now let us examine briefly in what senses the word "sarasvatī" has been used in the Ṛgveda. In this matter three points must be attended to: (1) the Ṛk we are now expounding, "pāvakā naḥ sarasvatī"; (2) the other Ṛks having Sarasvatī as their deity; (3) the ṛṣis who composed these Ṛks, and their lineages. We shall weigh these three matters.

In the sūkta now in hand, the Ṛks 10, 11 and 12 are mantras addressed to Sarasvatī. In the Ṛks 10 and 11, Sarasvatī is probably regarded as a deity and praised; in the 12th Ṛk, as the river. The Bhāṣyakāra Sāyaṇācārya explains Sarasvatī in the Ṛks 10–11 as the goddess of speech, and in the 12th Ṛk as the presiding deity of the river called Sarasvatī. Griffith explains "Sarasvatī" as the goddess of speech; but where "pāvakā" is given the sense "purifying with water," and where "ārṇa" [the word in Rik 3.12, "maho arṇaḥ"] is given the sense "river," "Sarasvatī" must mean a river, or the presiding deity of a river. Some modern scholars hold that "Sarasvatī" means the river Sindhu. But since the hermitage of the sage Madhucchandas, son of Viśvāmitra, who composed this Ṛk, was on the western bank of the present river Sarasvatī at Kurukṣetra — as stated in the Mahābhārata (Śalya-parva, adhyāya 43) — it is possible to conjecture that Madhucchandas praised this very river Sarasvatī: for when a person praises a river, it does not seem reasonable that he should leave aside the well-known river near the place where he lives and praise some other river of the same name far away.

In the second Maṇḍala, the Ṛks that have Sarasvatī as their deity — Ṛ. Saṃ. 2-30-8; 2-32-8; and 2-41-16 to 18 — were all composed by the ṛṣi Gṛtsamada, son of Śunahotra. This ṛṣi Gṛtsamada is understood to be the sixth in descent from the sage Atri (according to the book "Pravara and Gotra," No. 25 of the Mysore Government Oriental Library, as the source says); Viśvāmitra is the fifth in descent from Atri. In all, in eight Ṛks, this ṛṣi Gṛtsamada praises Sarasvatī… Page header: "Aṣṭaka 1, Adhyāya 1, Varga 6 · Ṛgveda-saṃhitā." Reference-numbers on this page re-read from the better scan (Oct 2026 numeral pass). English words as printed.

original p. 71

The ṛṣis who praise Sarasvatī: Gṛtsamada (continued), Devaśravas and Devavāta, Bharadvāja

Continuing from p. 70: …Gṛtsamada praises Sarasvatī. In Ṛ. Saṃ. 2-1-11 and 2-3-8 he praises Sarasvatī together with Iḷā and Bhāratī. In Ṛ. Saṃ. 2-35-5 he speaks of these three — that is, Iḷā, Sarasvatī and Bhāratī — as three goddesses. In Ṛ. Saṃ. 2-30-8 he praises Sarasvatī along with Indra and the Maruts. In Ṛ. Saṃ. 2-32-8 he speaks of Sarasvatī as a deity. In the 16th Ṛk of the sūkta 2-41 he describes Sarasvatī as a very large river and also a very large deity; and in the 18th Ṛk he describes her, with the word "ṛtāvarī" (that is, "ṛta" = water) as a river with abundant water. Seeing this, some Western scholars say, because she is spoken of as "a very large river," that she must be the Sindhu. But that is not right; for when a poet praises a river or a deity (even a small or ordinary one) it is common to describe it as very large. In Ṛ. Saṃ. 2-30-8 some think the ṛṣi Gṛtsamada praises Sarasvatī as the presiding deity of both rivers and the (cloud) lightning; but to say that one ṛṣi describes one and the same deity in different senses seems without reason.

The sūkta Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-23 has as ṛṣis Devaśravas and Devavāta, the sons of Bharata. According to the book "Gotra-Pravara" mentioned earlier, these ṛṣis are understood to be the sons of Viśvāmitra. Bharata is understood, from the same book, to be the sixth in descent from Atri, and Viśvāmitra the seventh [as the print says; compare the "fifth" for Viśvāmitra on p. 70 — the discrepancy is in the source and is recorded, not resolved]; both are descendants of Purūravas, the great-grandson of Atri (the print: "ಅತ್ರಿಯ ಮರಿಮಗನಾದ ಪುರೂರವನ ವಂಶಸ್ಥರು" — "descendants of Purūravas, Atri's great-grandson"). These ṛṣis in Ṛ. Saṃ. 3-23-4 say:

नि त्वा दधे वर आ पृथिव्या इळायास्पदे सुदिनत्वे अह्नाम् । दृषद्वत्यां मानुषा आपयायां सरस्वत्यां रेवदग्ने दिदीहि ॥ (ऋ. सं. ३-२३-४) ni tvā dadhe vara ā pṛthivyā iḷāyās pade sudinatve ahnām | dṛṣadvatyāṃ mānuṣā āpayāyāṃ sarasvatyāṃ revad agne didīhi || (ṛ. saṃ. 3-23-4) Gloss (mine): "I have set you down on the best place of the earth, on the footing of Iḷā, in the good days of the days; on the Dṛṣadvatī, among men, on the Āpayā, on the Sarasvatī: shine richly, O Agni."

Along with the river Sarasvatī they name two other rivers: Dṛṣadvatī and Āpayā. Dṛṣadvatī is the present river called Citrāṅga (the source's English: "the modern Chitrang, Chautag, or Chitang"); Āpayā is the present river called Apagā ("the modern Apaga"). Since both rivers lie in the neighbourhood of the river Sarasvatī, it can be said with confidence that Sarasvatī is not the Sindhu. Further, the hermitage of the sage Viśvāmitra, too, was on the west bank of this river Sarasvatī (in Kurukṣetra), as modern investigations show (the source adds: "see Dey's Geographical Dic."). All that has been said so far concerns the lineages of Atri and Viśvāmitra.

Now let us consider Bharadvāja and his lineage. The three Ṛks Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-49-7; 6-50-12; 6-52-6 all have, as their ṛṣi, Ṛjiśvā, the son of Bharadvāja. In the first and third of these three Ṛks, Sarasvatī is [described as] a river… Page header: "Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya-sahitā · Maṇḍala 1, Anuvāka 1, Sūkta 3." Reference-numbers marked [?] where unsure.

original p. 72

Sarasvatī as a river in the hymns of Bharadvāja, Vasiṣṭha and Śobhari

…the matter is stated clearly. In the second mantra, though the name of Sarasvatī is mentioned along with the names of the deities Rudra, Viṣṇu, Vāyu and Parjanya, Sarasvatī may be understood as a river; for in the two [other] Ṛks the ṛṣi says that Sarasvatī is a river, and in another Ṛk the same ṛṣi praises Sarasvatī as a river — which is only natural. The hermitage of Bharadvāja was at Prayāga (the source's English: "Allahabad"). Therefore Ṛjiśvā, son of Bharadvāja, must have praised a river near his own hermitage. The whole of Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-61 (14 Ṛks in all) by the ṛṣi Bharadvāja concerns Sarasvatī. Some Western scholars hold that the sense of several words in this sūkta applies to the river Sindhu; but since those words apply equally to the river Sarasvatī, there is no room for doubt.

The Ṛks in the seventh Maṇḍala — Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-9-5; 7-35-11; 7-36-6; 7-40-3; 7-95; 7-96 — are all by the ṛṣi Vasiṣṭha. The hermitage of Vasiṣṭha is understood to have been near Mount Abu (the source's English), a hill in the Āravalī mountain in Rājputānā. The first four mantras and the last two sūktas [of the group] praise Sarasvatī as a river. The words "sindhumātā" and "āsamudrāt" in these Ṛks apply especially to the river Sindhu, and so some say that it is the Sindhu that is praised in these mantras. This dispute cannot be completely set aside. Still, when speaking of one river, it is not impossible to compare another river with it, and to praise it with exaggeration.

In the eighth Maṇḍala, the Ṛks Ṛ. Saṃ. 8-21-17 and 18 are by the ṛṣi Śobhari, son of Kaṇva. In these Ṛks this ṛṣi describes the sacrifice that a king named Citra performed on the bank of the river Sarasvatī and praises that king's gifts. Since Śaunaka, in his Bṛhaddevatā (6-58 to 62), says that this king Citra performed a sacrifice at Kurukṣetra, the river must be the nearby Sarasvatī. And:

पूषा विष्णुर्हवनं मे सरस्वत्यवन्तु सप्त सिन्धवः । आपो वातः पर्वतासो वनस्पतिः शृणोतु पृथिवी हवम् ॥ (ऋ. सं. ८-५४-९) pūṣā viṣṇur havanaṃ me sarasvaty avantu sapta sindhavaḥ | āpo vātaḥ parvatāso vanaspatiḥ śṛṇotu pṛthivī havam || (ṛ. saṃ. 8-54-9) Gloss (mine): "May Pūṣan, Viṣṇu, Sarasvatī, the seven rivers, help my invocation; the Waters, the Wind, the Mountains, the Tree-lord — may Earth hear my call."

In this Ṛk, Sarasvatī is also mentioned among the deities Pūṣan, Viṣṇu, Sarasvatī, the Seven Rivers (sapta-sindhavaḥ), the Waters, the Wind, the Mountains, the Lord of the Forest (Vanaspati) and Earth. Likewise in Ṛ. Saṃ. 9-67-32, the ṛṣi of that mantra, Vasiṣṭha or Pavitra, has used the word "Sarasvatī." Here Sarasvatī may be taken in either sense, as a deity or as a river. In Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-30-12, it is clearly stated which river is meant by "Sarasvatī" … Page header: "Aṣṭaka 1, Adhyāya 1, Varga 6 · Ṛgveda-saṃhitā." Reference-numbers marked [?] where unsure. original p. 73

Sarasvatī among the rivers (Ṛ. 10-75); the ten Āprī-sūktas (opening of the list)

Continuing from p. 72, "…it is clearly stated which river is meant by 'Sarasvatī':" In Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-64-9 the ṛṣi of that mantra, Gaya (of the lineage of Atri), speaks of Sarasvatī in the company of the rivers Sindhu and Sarayū (the source's English: "Gogra"). And:

इमं मे गङ्गे यमुने सरस्वति शुतुद्रि स्तोमं सचता परुष्ण्या । असिक्न्या मरुद्वृधे वितस्तयार्जीकीये शृणुह्या सुषोमया ॥ (ऋ. सं. १०-७५-५) imaṃ me gaṅge yamune sarasvati śutudri stomaṃ sacatā paruṣṇyā | asiknyā marudvṛdhe vitastayārjīkīye śṛṇuhy ā suṣomayā || (ṛ. saṃ. 10-75-5) Gloss (mine): "O Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī, Śutudri — attend to this my praise, together with Paruṣṇī; with Asiknī, O Marudvṛdhā, with Vitastā, O Ārjīkīyā, hear, together with Suṣomā."

In this Ṛk the river Sarasvatī is named together with Gaṅgā (the Ganges), Yamunā (the Jamna), Śutudri (the Sutlej), Paruṣṇī (the Ravi), Asiknī (the Chinab), Vitastā (the Jhelam), Marudvṛdhā (the United Stream of the Jhelam and Chenab), Ārjīkīyā (the Bias) and Suṣomā (the Indus) — all in the source's English — and from this it is plain that the river Sarasvatī is one distinct river of her own and is not the Sindhu. The entire sūkta in which the above Ṛk occurs is about rivers: all the Ṛks of this sūkta [the number is printed "9" — read with caution] have rivers for their deities. The ṛṣi of this sūkta is Sindhukṣit, the son of Priyamedha.

Sarasvatī is spoken of in the Āprī-sūktas as one of the three goddesses called "tisro devyaḥ." In the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā there are ten sūktas that are called Āprī-sūktas. In Śaunaka's Anuvākānukramaṇī the particulars of these sūktas are given thus:

श्लोकस्यास्य यथासंख्यं सूक्तानि दश वै विदुः । न आ वहाग्न आ वहाद्य राजसेत्यग्निर्नि च । समित्समित्सु शोचिषे जुषस्व विश्वतस्तथा । इमां मे अद्य मन्विमा यथर्षिपक्ष आप्रियः ॥ वसिष्ठशुनकौ विना समिद्धः सर्वपक्षता । जुषस्वादिद्वितीयया तनूनपाद्विरोधिता । यजुः श्रुतौ तथाश्रुतेः समिद्धसूक्तमध्यतः । प्रजापतेः पशोः सदा भवेयुरद्य मन्विमाः ॥ इतीरितं हि बह्वृचैर्यथर्षि वेति सूत्रतः ॥

ślokasyāsya yathā-saṃkhyaṃ sūktāni daśa vai viduḥ | na ā vahāgna ā vahādya rājasety agnir ni ca | samit-samit-su śociṣe juṣasva viśvatas tathā | imāṃ me adya manvimā yatharṣi-pakṣa āpriyaḥ || vasiṣṭha-śunakau vinā samiddhaḥ sarva-pakṣatā | juṣasvādi-dvitīyayā tanūnapād-virodhitā | yajuḥ śrutau tathā-śruteḥ samiddha-sūkta-madhyataḥ | prajāpateḥ paśoḥ sadā bhaveyur adya manvimāḥ | itīritaṃ hi bahvṛcair yathā-ṛṣi veti sūtrataḥ ||

Outline of the sense (not a line-by-line translation — the verses are a compressed mnemonic, and several words are garbled in the print): the verses state that there are ten such sūktas, "in order of number," and give them by their opening words ("na ā vaha," "ā vaha," "rājasi," "agnir nihitaḥ," and so on); they note which of them are by Vasiṣṭha and Śunaka (Śaunaka); they note how the Yajus and Śruti texts treat "samiddha" in the middle of the sūkta; and they say that, as the Ṛgvedins' sūtra puts it, the sūktas are recited "according to the ṛṣi."

Of the sūktas listed above, the sūktas numbered 1–2 have 12 and 13 Ṛks; all the rest have 11 Ṛks. The deities of these 11 Ṛks are as follows:

Ṛk Deity (Sanskrit as printed) Meaning

In the first sūkta with 12 Ṛks, the deity Narāśaṃsa is also present; in the second sūkta, with 13 Ṛks, both Narāśaṃsa and Indra are deities; therefore, in place of the 11 Ṛks of the other sūktas, these have 12 and 13. In the other matters there is no difference — only the metres and the ṛṣis differ. In the animal sacrifice (paśuyāga), while praising Agni (the "samiddha-agni") and while performing the eleven prayāja homas, these sūktas are recited. In these sūktas, "tisro devyaḥ" means the praise of the three goddesses Iḷā, Sarasvatī, Bhāratī. The chief point to be noted here is that Agni is worshipped in three forms: on earth, in the atmosphere, and in heaven. Since Bhāratī indicates the rays of the Sun, this deity (that is, the Sun) is the form of Agni in heaven. original p. 75

"tisro devyaḥ"; Rigvedic verses that treat Sarasvatī as a deity rather than a river

Continuing from p. 74, "Sarasvatī … for lightning, the one presiding…" …Because Sarasvatī is described in many places as a presiding deity of the lightning (vidyud-abhimānī-devatā), this Sarasvatī is the form of Agni in the atmosphere. Because the goddess Iḷā gives to the people on earth wealth and the like and long life, this goddess is the form of Agni on earth: such is the signification of these three, Iḷā, Sarasvatī and Bhāratī. The ṛṣis praise these three goddesses, asking them to come to the sacrificial altar and sit on the "barhis" (spread darbha-grass).

Here are some examples of verses in which the ṛṣis praise Sarasvatī as a deity other than a river: Page header: "Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya-sahitā · Maṇḍala 1, Anuvāka 1, Sūkta 3." Reference-numbers marked [?] where unsure. English words and the bibliographic list are as printed in the source.

  1. तान्पूर्वया निविदा हूमहे वयं भगं मित्रमदितिं दक्षमस्रिधम् । अर्यमणं वरुणं सोममश्विना सरस्वती नः सुभगा मयस्करत् ॥ (ऋ. सं. १-८९-३) tān pūrvayā nividā hūmahe vayaṃ bhagaṃ mitram aditiṃ dakṣam asridham | aryamaṇaṃ varuṇaṃ somam aśvinā sarasvatī naḥ subhagā mayas karat || (ṛ. saṃ. 1-89-3) Gloss: "Those (gods) we invoke with the ancient invocation — Bhaga, Mitra, Aditi, the undecaying Dakṣa, Aryaman, Varuṇa, Soma, the Aśvins; may fortunate Sarasvatī make us happy." (The source's remark:) In this Ṛk Sarasvatī is the goddess of speech, or the presiding deity of lightning.

  2. सरस्वति त्वमस्माँ अविड्ढि मरुत्वती धृषती जेषि शत्रून् । (ऋ. सं. २-३०-८) sarasvati tvam asmāṁ aviḍḍhi marutvatī dhṛṣatī jeṣi śatrūn | (ṛ. saṃ. 2-30-8) Gloss: "O Sarasvatī, protect us; accompanied by the Maruts, bold, you conquer the foes."

  3. सरस्वती शृणवन्यज्ञियासो धाता रयिं सहवीरं तुरासः । (ऋ. सं. ३-५४-१३) sarasvatī śṛṇavanyajñiyāso dhātā rayiṃ sahavīraṃ turāsaḥ | (ṛ. saṃ. 3-54-13) Gloss: "May Sarasvatī hear — (the gods) worthy of sacrifice — bestowing wealth with heroes, the swift conqueror." [tentative; "turāsaḥ" as printed, re-read from the better scan]

(The source's remark on (2) and (3):) In these Ṛks Sarasvatī is regarded either as a river or as the presiding deity of lightning.

  1. दमूनसो अपसो ये सुहस्ता वृष्णः पत्नीर्नद्यो विभ्वतष्टाः । सरस्वती बृहद्दिवोत राका दशस्यन्तीर्वरिवस्यन्तु शुभ्राः ॥ (ऋ. सं. ५-४२-१२) damūnaso apaso ye suhastā vṛṣṇaḥ patnīr nadyo vibhvataṣṭāḥ | sarasvatī bṛhaddivota rākā daśasyantīr varivasyantu śubhrāḥ || (ṛ. saṃ. 5-42-12) Gloss: "(…) the wives of the bull, the rivers shaped by the Skilful One; may Sarasvatī, Bṛhaddivā and Rākā, the bright ones, giving, grant wide room." [tentative; the first half is hard for me to render with confidence]

  2. आ नो दिवो बृहतः पर्वतादा सरस्वती यजता गन्तु यज्ञम् । (ऋ. सं. ५-४३-११) ā no divo bṛhataḥ parvatād ā sarasvatī yajatā gantu yajñam | (ṛ. saṃ. 5-43-11) Gloss: "May worshipful Sarasvatī come to our sacrifice from heaven, from the great mountain."

  3. उभा नासत्या रुद्रो अध ग्नाः पूषा भगः सरस्वती जुषन्त । (ऋ. सं. ५-४६-२) ubhā nāsatyā rudro adha gnāḥ pūṣā bhagaḥ sarasvatī juṣanta | (ṛ. saṃ. 5-46-2) Gloss: "May both Nāsatyas, Rudra, the goddesses' wives, Pūṣan, Bhaga, Sarasvatī be pleased."

(The source's remark:) In these three Ṛks, too, Sarasvatī is the presiding deity of lightning. Griffith holds that in the first of these three Ṛks Sarasvatī is some one river — "Sindhu or Sarasvatī" — and that in the 2nd and 3rd [Ṛks of the group] the deity is clear. K. C. Caṭṭopādhyāya says that Ṛks 1–2 [of the group] apply to the Sindhu. These three Ṛks too, it is said, were composed by the descendants of the ṛṣi Atri. For the first Ṛk… (continues on the next page)

The deity-verses (concluded); where the river Sarasvatī flowed

…for the first Ṛk, Atri, or Atri's son Bhauma, is the ṛṣi; for the second Ṛk, Atri; for the third, Pratikṣatra, a descendant of Atri. In the second Ṛk Sarasvatī is addressed as having come from heaven ("divaḥ") and from the great mountain ("parvatāt") — [as the print has it]. In the first Ṛk, since the word "patnīḥ" ("wives") appears, the Bhāṣyakāra has regarded Sarasvatī and the other rivers as the wives of Indra.

  1. अग्निरिन्द्रो वरुणो मित्रो अर्यमा वायुः पूषा सरस्वती सजोषसः । (ऋ. सं. १०-६५-१) agnir indro varuṇo mitro aryamā vāyuḥ pūṣā sarasvatī sajoṣasaḥ | (ṛ. saṃ. 10-65-1) Gloss: "Agni, Indra, Varuṇa, Mitra, Aryaman, Vāyu, Pūṣan, Sarasvatī, in concert."

  2. विश्वे देवासः शृणवन्वचांसि मे सरस्वती सह धीभिः पुरंध्या । (ऋ. सं. १०-६५-१३) viśve devāsaḥ śṛṇavan vacāṃsi me sarasvatī saha dhībhiḥ puraṃdhyā | (ṛ. saṃ. 10-65-13) Gloss: "May the All-gods hear my words, and Sarasvatī with her thoughts and her plenty."

(The source's remark:) In these two Ṛks, too, Sarasvatī is the goddess of speech.

  1. यत्सारामं व्यपिबः शचीभिः सरस्वती त्वा मघवन्नभिष्णक् । (ऋ. सं. १०-१३१-५) yat sārāmaṃ vy apibaḥ śacībhiḥ sarasvatī tvā maghavann abhiṣṇak | (ṛ. saṃ. 10-131-5) Gloss: "When you drank the [sārāma-drink?] with your powers, O Maghavan, Sarasvatī tended you." [tentative; "sārāmam" is not rendered with confidence]

(The source's remark:) Since in this Ṛk Sarasvatī is spoken of as accompanying Indra, she may be understood either as the presiding deity of lightning or as the goddess of speech.

  1. गर्भं धेहि सिनीवालि गर्भं धेहि सरस्वति । (ऋ. सं. १०-१८४-२) garbhaṃ dhehi sinīvāli garbhaṃ dhehi sarasvati | (ṛ. saṃ. 10-184-2) Gloss: "Set the embryo, O Sinīvālī; set the embryo, O Sarasvatī."

(The source's remark:) Here it is only fitting to speak of Sarasvatī as the goddess of speech [as the print says — "vāg-devatā," though the verse is a prayer for conception].

Where the river Sarasvatī flowed. We shall now set out briefly, for those who wish to know, the discussion of where the river Sarasvatī flowed in that age. This account has been written following the publications: (1) R. D. Oldham in Journal of Asiatic Society Bengal, 1886, page 322; (2) C. F. Oldham, Journal of Royal Asiatic Society, 1893, page 51; (3) Maps of the Cambridge History of India, Vol. I, "Ancient India"; (4) Maps of Punjab published by the Surveyor-General of India; (5) "Ancient India as described by Megasthenes and Arrian." All as printed. In that age the river Sarasvatī was one large river. It arose in the Sirmur (the source's English: "Sismur") range in the Himālayas and flowed to the west and slightly south. At its source five small streams (small watercourses carrying water) joined and then flowed on as this river; for this reason it must have had the name "Pañcajātā." After flowing a little distance, a river called Dṛṣadvatī (the modern Chitrang) joined it, coming from the east. Āpayā is a tributary of the Dṛṣadvatī. The Sarasvatī of that time was to the south of the present Sarasvatī river (the source adds: rivers that flow in desert regions often change their beds). Into the present Sarasvatī river two small streams called Mārkaṇḍā (the source's English: "Markand") and Gaggar ("Ghaggar") … Page header: "Aṣṭaka 1, Adhyāya 1, Varga 6 · Ṛgveda-saṃhitā." English words are as printed in the source. The Ṛg-vedic numbers in the list of senses of "vāja" below are in small Kannada numerals and they could not be read reliably; they are omitted rather than guessed, and the list should be completed from the page.

original p. 77

The course of the Sarasvatī (concluded); "vājebhiḥ"

Continuing from p. 76, "…two small streams, Mārkaṇḍā and Gaggar…" …these streams join her. Afterwards the Sarasvatī flowed on towards the south and west and finally joined the sea. The bed of the dried-up river now called Hakra (as printed) must have been the bed of the Sarasvatī of that time. It may have merged in the Sindhu by uniting with the river now called the Sutlej, or may have gone directly and joined the Sindhu. In that age the Sindhu lay far to the east of where it now is, and joined the sea near the gulf called the Rann of Kach (as printed). The scholar Max Müller, on the basis of the word "āsamudrāt" in Ṛ. Saṃ. 7-95-2, holds that this Sarasvatī river went directly and joined the sea. Since the river flowed through sandy country before reaching the sea, it may well have been lost in the desert before reaching it (see Muir's Sanskrit Texts, Vol. II, p. 393, as printed). The account that the river was lost in the desert is given in the Mahābhārata (Vana-parva, in the description of the Tīrthayātrā) and also in the Manu-saṃhitā (1-21 [as printed]). For all these reasons it may be said that the present river Sarasuti is the Sarasvatī of old.

वाजेभिः (vājebhiḥ) — This word is used in this Ṛk in the sense "anna, āhāra" ("food"); there is the Taittirīya Śruti sentence "annaṃ vai vājaḥ" (अन्नं वै वाजः — "food indeed is 'vāja'"). Western scholars say that this word is used in many Ṛks in many different senses. Some of them are given here English as printed, with the source's Ṛg-vedic references, re-read from the better scan:

  1. Power, strength — Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-27-8; 1-110-6; 3-25-3; 4-22-3; 5-15-5; 6-25-11 &c.
  2. Swiftnets [sic] (of the steeds) — Ṛ. Saṃ. 5-85-2; 10-39-10.
  3. Combat — Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-4-4; 1-7-4; 2-23-13 &c.
  4. Refreshment, food, nourishment — Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-91-18; 6-24-3; 10-5-4; 10-96-9 &c.
  5. Offering, food or drink of offering — Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-36-2; 3-12-9; 4-3-15; 5-9-2; 6-45-29 &c.
  6. Horse — Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-52-1; 2-1-12; 3-2-3; 4-29-1 &c.
  7. One of the three Rubhus [sic] — Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-161-6; 4-33-3; 7-48-2 &c.
  8. All the three Rubhus [sic] — Ṛ. Saṃ. 10-23-2; 10-74-10 &c.

Grassmann has given one long list for the various senses of this word, which occurs in many Ṛks; since it is very extensive, and since it is fitting to explain those senses in the respective places, there is no need to write it here. original p. 78

"vājinīvatī," "yajñam," "vaṣṭu," "dhiyāvasuḥ"

वाजिनीवती (vājinīvatī) — The sense of this word follows that of the word "vājebhiḥ" given above. For it, Rāmanātha gives "Bestower of food"; Benfey, "filled up or rich with offerings"; Geldner, "rich with reward"; Rosen, "provided with food"; Ludwig, "rich with steed"; and the author of the Vedārtha-yatna, "Mounted on a charger" all as printed. Some say "vājinī" means the fruit-bearing land on a river bank that produces food, and "vājinīvatī" a river that gives people food and the like by supplying water to such fruitful land.

यज्ञम् (yajñam) — The word "yajña" is read among the fifteen words in the Nirukta (Ni. 3-19). This word can be explained in two ways: (1) the worship of a deity by hymns of praise and the like; (2) a special rite performed by the subsidiary and sub-subsidiary rites, by the recitation of mantras, by offering up an animal, and by many homas. It is this second kind of rite that is generally described in the Vedas by the word "yajña."

वष्टु (vaṣṭu) — This word is the imperative (loṭ) third-person singular of the root "vaś kāntau" (to desire). The Bhāṣyakāra, giving the root the sense "apekṣā" ("expectation, wish"), states the main sense as "nirvahatv iti arthaḥ" — "let her bring (the sacrifice) to completion with all its parts." To support this he quotes the Aitareya Āraṇyaka sentence "yajñaṃ vaṣṭv iti yad āha yajñaṃ vahatv ity eva tad āha" (यज्ञं वष्ट्विति यदाह यज्ञं वहत्वित्येव तदाह — "when it says 'let her desire the sacrifice,' it says 'let her carry the sacrifice'," ऐ. आ. १-१-४). Geldner and Grassmann give "desire, wish for, make efforts, carry on to completion" ; the last sense is the right one here.

धियावसुः (dhiyāvasuḥ) — The Bhāṣyakāra explains this word thus: "dhiyāvasuḥ karma-prāpty-adhana-nimitta-bhūtā | vāg-devatāyās tathāvidhaṃ dhana-nimittatvam āraṇyaka-kāṇḍe śrutyā vyākhyātam | yajñaṃ vaṣṭu dhiyāvasur iti vāg vai dhiyāvasuḥ" (धियावसुः कर्मप्राप्त्यधननिमित्तभूता । वाग्देवतायास्तथाविधं धननिमित्तत्वमारण्यककाण्डे श्रुत्या व्याख्यातं । यज्ञं वष्टु धियावसुरिति वाग्वै धियावसुः — ऐ. आ. १-१-४ — "Dhiyāvasuḥ: she who is the occasion of wealth to be gained by ritual action; that the goddess of speech is the occasion of wealth of this kind is explained by Śruti in the Āraṇyaka section: 'yajñaṃ vaṣṭu dhiyāvasuḥ' — speech indeed is dhiyāvasuḥ"). That is: "dhiyāvasu" means she who is the cause of the attaining of wealth, lordship and the like, obtained through sacrifices and other rites; the Bhāṣyakāra also quotes the Aitareya-Āraṇyaka sentence "yajñaṃ vaṣṭu" etc. to say that the goddess of speech is the cause of the attainment of wealth. And in considering the formation of the word he says: "dhiyā karmaṇā vasu yasyāḥ sakāśād bhavati sā dhiyāvasuḥ" (धिया कर्मणा वसु यस्याः सकाशाद्भवति सा धियावसुः) — the deity from whom the wealth that is to be obtained as the fruit of rites comes is called "dhiyāvasuḥ." Western scholars explain it with such words as : "Supporter of all by wisdom, recompenser of worship or religious ceremonies, bestower of riches, source of wealth, rich in sense or intellect, one rewarding for devotion excellent-minded." This word is used in the Ṛgveda only in eight Ṛks: Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-3-10; 1-58-9; 10-60-5; 1-61-16; 1-62-13; 1-64-15; 3-3-2 [seven references, as printed, for "eight"]. original p. 79

Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā for Rik 3.10 (Kannada); Sūkta 3, Eleventh Mantra: Saṃhitā and Pada text

॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥ - "Pāvakā" — "pāvaṃ kāyatīti pāvakā": from the root "kai" ("kai gai rai śabde," to sound) with "ka" after an upasarga-less word (आतोऽनुपसर्गे कः, āto 'nupasarge kaḥ, पा. ३-२-३); the substitution of "ā" for the final of the root by आदेच उपदेशेऽशिति (ād eca upadeśe 'śiti, पा. ६-१-४५); elision of the final "ā" before the affix (आतो लोप इटि च, āto lopa iṭi ca, पा. ६-४-६९ [as printed]); the feminine "ṭāp" (अजाद्यतष्टाप्, ajādy-ataṣ ṭāp, पा. ४-१-४) → "pāvakā"; being a kṛt-ending compound-member, the accent of the second member is retained by गतिकारकोपपदात्कृत् (पा. ६-२-१३९) as an end-acute. Alternatively, if "pūñ" ("he purifies") is intended, the affix "ṇvul" (ण्वुल्तृचौ, ṇvul-tṛcau, पा. ३-१-१३३) is added, and "yu/vu" are replaced by "ana/aka" (युवोरनाकौ, yuvor anākau, पा. ७-१-१), with the guṇa and "av-" substitution, giving "pāvaka," then "ṭāp" for the feminine "pāvakā." A difficulty is noted: by प्रत्ययस्थात्कात्पूर्वस्यात इदाप्यसुपः (pratyayasthāt kāt pūrvasyāta idāpy asupaḥ, पा. ७-३-४४) the "a" before "ka" would become "i" ("pāvikā"); the answer is that the non-occurrence of "i" in "pāvakā" is Vedic usage, by पावकादीनां छन्दसि प्रत्ययस्थात्कादित्वं नेति वाच्यम् [the print is garbled here; given as read]. The end-acute is likewise accepted as Vedic. - "Sarasvatī" — from "sṛ" with the Uṇādi "asun" → "saras"; the affix is "n"-marked (nit), so the first syllable is acute. The following "matup" and "ṅīp" are "p"-marked and unaccented.

Sūkta 3, The Eleventh Mantra

॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥

चो॒द॒यि॒त्री सू॒नृता॑नां॒ चेतं॑ती सुमती॒नां । य॒ज्ञं द॑धे॒ सर॑स्वती ॥११॥

codayitrī́ sūnṛ́tānāṃ cétaṃtī sumatīnā́ṃ | yajñáṃ dadhe sárasvatī ||11||

॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥ Page header: "Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya-sahitā · Maṇḍala 1, Anuvāka 1, Sūkta 3." Sanskrit printed in Kannada script, rendered letter by letter; [?] where unclear.

चोदयित्री । सूनृतानाम् । चेतन्ती । सुमतीनाम् । यज्ञम् । दधे । सरस्वती ॥११॥

original p. 80

Rik 3.11: Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya, grammar, Pada-meanings, Bhāvārtha, English rendering; Special topic (opening)

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥

यो सरस्वती सेयमिमं यज्ञं दधे । धारितवती । कीदृशी । सूनृतानां प्रियाणां सत्यवाक्यानां चोदयित्री प्रेरयित्री । सुमतीनां शोभनबुद्धियुक्तानामनुष्ठातॄणां चेतन्ती । तदीयमनुष्ठेयं ज्ञापयन्ती ॥ yo [print; "yā" would be expected] sarasvatī seyam imaṃ yajñaṃ dadhe | dhāritavatī | kīdṛśī | sūnṛtānāṃ priyāṇāṃ satya-vākyānāṃ codayitrī prerayitrī | sumatīnāṃ śobhana-buddhi-yuktānām anuṣṭhātṝṇāṃ cetantī | tadīyam anuṣṭheyaṃ jñāpayantī ||

Translation: "That Sarasvatī — she has taken up ('dadhe' = 'dhāritavatī') this sacrifice. What kind of one? 'Codayitrī' — the inciter, the impeller, of 'sūnṛtānām' — of pleasant, true utterances (or of those who speak them); 'cetantī' — the one who makes known, to the 'sumatīnām' — those of good understanding, the performers — what is to be performed by them." The print's first word reads "yo"; the sense needs "yā" ("who"), and the print is recorded as it stands.

Grammar within the Bhāṣya characterized; the print is partly garbled in the middle, and no reading of the unclear stretch is given: "Codayitrī" — root "cud" (to impel), "ṇic," then "tṛc"; "c"-marked, so the penultimate is acute (चित्त्वादन्तोदात्तः); "ṅīp" (ऋन्नेभ्यो ङीप्, पा. ४-१-५); the feminine ending is acute by उदात्तयणो हल्पूर्वात् (udāttayaṇo hal-pūrvāt, पा. ६-१-१७४). "Sūnṛtānām" — "ūna parihāṇe" (to lessen) with "kvip"; "sūnīti priyam ucyate" — "sūn" denotes the pleasant; "ṛtaṃ satyam"; hence "sūnṛtam" = pleasant and true; the second member's acute follows the rule for compounds beginning with "para-ādi" in the Veda (बहुलमुत्तरपदादिः, as printed [?]). "Cetantī" — root "citī saṃjñāne" (to perceive); the "śap" is elided and "p"-marked, so unaccented; the stem's own accent remains; "ṅīp" etc. "Sumatīnām" — "mati" is first-syllable-acute; the genitive-plural ending's accent (पा. ६-१-१७७).

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥

सरस्वती (sarasvatī) — the goddess Sarasvatī | सूनृतानाम् (sūnṛtānām) — [of] pleasant and true words, or [of] men who speak such words | चोदयित्री (codayitrī) — one who impels | सुमतीनाम् (sumatīnām) — (those who are devoted to sacrifices and the like) men of good understanding | चेतन्ती (cetantī) — one who makes (them) know (what is to be done in good works) | (such Sarasvatī) यज्ञम् (yajñam) — the sacrifice (that we are performing) | दधे (dadhe) — has taken up (carries through).

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

The goddess Sarasvatī, whom we praise, is she who impels men to speak pleasant and true words, or who inspires those who speak the truth to engage in good works, and who, by making known to men of good understanding what is to be done, helps them in doing right. May such a Sarasvatī bring the sacrifice that we perform to a faultless completion.

English Translation (printed in English in the source itself):

"Saraswati, the inspirer of those who speak only the truth and instructress of the right-minded has supported the sacrifice."

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥

This mantra is used in the sacrifice called Sautrāmaṇī; and also in the Vaiśvadeva, the Ukhāsambharaṇa (which, the source adds in English, "takes place at the new and full moon days") and the Ekāṣṭakā (the eighth day after full moon). Chiefly, this mantra is used in the rite called Vaiśvadeva, in the offering of the bali to Sarasvatī. Page header: "Aṣṭaka 1, Adhyāya 1, Varga 6 · Ṛgveda-saṃhitā." English words are as printed in the source. Nirukta reference-numbers re-read from the better scan, Oct 2026 numeral pass.

original p. 81

Special topics on Rik 3.11; Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā (opening)

चोदयित्री (codayitrī) — A form derived from the root "cud" ("cuda preraṇe," to impel); the sense is "she who impels." Western scholars explain it with the words : "Inspire, incite, rouse, stimulate, furnish, quickly, hasten, hurry, stir, agitate, encourage."

सूनृतानाम् (sūnṛtānām) — The word "sūnṛta" is read both among the sixteen words that indicate "uṣas" (dawn) (Ni. 2-19) and among the twenty-eight words that indicate "anna" (food) (Ni. 3-9) [re-read from the better scan, Oct 2026]. This word is derived from the word "ṛta," which means "true, truth." Hence, in the Ṛgveda, Western scholars explain the word "sūnṛta" with such words as : "One delighting in truth, good word, agreeable speech, truth, song, receiving good qualities, joy-giving, glorious deed."

चेतन्ती (cetantī) — The sense of this word is, with a slight addition, the same as that of "codayitrī"; for it, such senses as "Perceive, conceive, understand, inspire" may be given.

सुमतीनाम् (sumatīnām) — This word is formed from the root "man" (to think). For it one may give : "Think, meditate, contemplate, imagine, observe, believe, regard." In this Ṛk, for this word the senses "those who have good understanding," "those devoted to good deeds, or those who do them," "right-thinking, right-minded" may be given.

The chief import of this Ṛk: the goddess Sarasvatī impels men to speak true words and to do good works, and makes people's minds devoted to good activities. Therefore, she gives us good understanding in the sacrifice that we are now performing, makes that sacrifice reach completion with all its parts, and favours us so that we obtain its fruit.

॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥ "Codayitrī": to the root "cud preraṇe" the affix "ṇic" is added; the penultimate light vowel takes guṇa, giving "codi-"; then "tṛc" (ण्वुल्तृचौ, ṇvul-tṛcau, पा. ३-१-१३३); "iṭ" comes to it by आर्धधातुकस्येड्वलादेः (पा. ७-२-३५); the "i" of "codi" takes guṇa (सार्वधातुकार्धधातुकयोः, पा. ७-३-८४) and "ay" by एचोऽयवायावः (eco 'yavāyāvaḥ, पा. ६-१-७८) → "codayitṛ"; for the feminine, ऋन्नेभ्यो ङीप् (ṛnnebhyo ṅīp, पा. ४-१-५) — "ṅīp" after words ending in "ṛ" and "n" — and then यणादेशः (the semivowel substitution "ṛ → r") … Page header: "Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya-sahitā · Maṇḍala 1, Anuvāka 1, Sūkta 3." This page is dense accent-derivation in Kannada prose, repeating the Sanskrit grammar of p. 80. Per the standing convention it is characterized, not translated line by line; the sūtras are kept. Some details are garbled in the print and are not given.

original p. 82

Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā for Rik 3.11 concluded — characterized

Continuing "codayitrī": …"codayitr + ī" → "codayitrī". Since "tṛc" is "c"-marked (चितः, पा. ६-१-१६३) the last syllable is acute; the feminine ending then takes the acute by उदात्तयणो हल्पूर्वात् (udāttayaṇo hal-pūrvāt, पा. ६-१-१७४) — when an "ṇ"-substituted semivowel following a consonant stands for an acute vowel, the following case-ending is acute — hence "ī" is acute.

"Sūnṛtānām" — "ūna parihāṇau" (to lessen), with "kvip" by क्विप् च (पा. ३-२-७६) → "ūn"; "sutarām ūnayati apriyam" — "he who most completely removes what is unpleasant" — so "sūn" is a word for "the pleasant"; "ṛtam" = true; "sūn ca tad ṛtaṃ ca" — a karmadhāraya compound, "sūnṛtam." Here, by परादिश्छन्दसि बहुलम् (parādiś chandasi bahulam, पा. ६-२-१९९), in the Veda the beginning of the latter member is variably acute; so the first syllable of the second member is acute. Through "āyasmayādīni chandasi" (आयस्मयादीनि छन्दसि, पा. १-४-२०) the words "ayasmaya" and others in the Veda get the "bha" and "pada" labels as suitable; hence the "bha"-label arises, and since there is no "pada"-label, न लोपः प्रातिपदिकान्तस्य (na lopaḥ prātipadikāntasya, पा. ८-२-७) — the elision of the final "n" of a stem — does not apply to the "n" of "sūn."

"Cetantī" — root "citī saṃjñāne"; in place of "laṭ" the "śatṛ" affix (लटः शतृशानचावप्रथमासमानाधिकरणे, पा. ३-२-१२४) → "cit + at"; "śap" comes, then guṇa of the light penultimate, and by अतो गुणे (पा. ६-१-९७) the single form → "cetat"; "śatṛ" is "uk"-marked (उगितश्च, ugitaś ca, पा. ४-१-६), so "ṅīp" for the feminine, giving "cetat + ī"; by आच्छीनद्योर्नुम् (āc chīnadyor num, पा. ७-१-८०) "num" is the augment, optionally, when "śī" or "nadī"-labelled endings follow; "cetantī" results; by हल्ङ्याब्भ्यो दीर्घात्… (पा. ६-१-६८) the elision. Both "śap" and "ṅīp" being "p"-marked, they are unaccented; the "śatṛ" affix is accented on the first syllable by तास्यनुदात्तेन्ङिददुपदेशाल्लसार्वधातुकमनुदात्तमहन्वनोर्ङित् (पा. ६-१-१८६) [as printed, garbled] and the stem's own accent remains; the final vowel of "cetat," by धातोः (पा. ६-१-१६२) — the last vowel of a root is acute — is acute on the "e."

"Sumatīnām" — "śobhanā matiḥ yeṣāṃ te" — "those with good understanding," a bahuvrīhi; by नञ्सुभ्याम् (पा. ६-२-१७२) the second member is end-acute; after it, when the genitive plural ending is added, "nuṭ" is the augment and the vowel is lengthened — "sumatīnām." Here, by नामन्यतरस्याम् (nāmany atarasyām, पा. ६-१-१७७), in the case where the "matup"-final is elided... — if the stem is end-acute, the genitive plural ending "nām" is acute; thus the "nām" of "sumatīnām" is acute. ॥११॥ Page header: "Aṣṭaka 1, Adhyāya 1, Varga 6 · Ṛgveda-saṃhitā." Accent-marks not reproduced; see the note at Rik 3.5. Sanskrit printed in Kannada script, rendered letter by letter.

original p. 83

Sūkta 3, Twelfth Mantra: Saṃhitā, Pada, Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya, Pada-meanings

Sūkta 3, The Twelfth Mantra

॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥

म॒हो अर्णः॒ सर॑स्वती॒ प्र चे॑तयति के॒तुना॑ । धियो॒ विश्वा वि रा॑जति ॥१२॥

mahó arṇaḥ sárasvatī prá cetayati ketúnā | dhiyo víśvā ví rājati ||12||

॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥

महः । अर्णः । सरस्वती । प्र । चेतयति । केतुना । धियः । विश्वाः । वि । राजति ॥१२॥

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥

द्विविधा हि सरस्वती विग्रहवद्देवता नदीरूपा च । तत्र पूर्वाभ्यामृग्भ्यां विग्रहवती प्रतिपादिता । अनया तु नदीरूपा प्रतिपाद्यते । तादृशी सरस्वती केतुना कर्मणा प्रवाहरूपेण महो अर्णः प्रभूतमुदकं प्र चेतयति । प्रकर्षेण ज्ञापयति । किंच । स्वकीयेन देवतारूपेण विश्वा धियः सर्वाण्यनुष्ठातृप्रज्ञानानि विराजति । विशेषेण दीपयति । अनुष्ठानविषया बुद्धिः । सर्वोत्पादयतीत्यर्थः । dvividhā hi sarasvatī vigrahavad-devatā nadī-rūpā ca | tatra pūrvābhyām ṛgbhyāṃ vigrahavatī pratipāditā | anayā tu nadī-rūpā pratipādyate | tādṛśī sarasvatī ketunā karmaṇā pravāha-rūpeṇa maho arṇaḥ prabhūtam udakaṃ pra cetayati | prakarṣeṇa jñāpayati | kiṃca | svakīyena devatā-rūpeṇa viśvā dhiyaḥ sarvāṇy anuṣṭhātṛ-prajñānāni virājati | viśeṣeṇa dīpayati | anuṣṭhāna-viṣayā buddhiḥ | sarvotpādayatīty arthaḥ |

Translation: "Sarasvatī is indeed of two kinds: a deity with a body (a goddess), and in the form of a river. Of these, the two preceding Ṛks presented her as the embodied one; by this Ṛk she is presented in river form. Such a Sarasvatī, 'ketunā' — by her action, in the form of her flow — makes known ('pra cetayati') 'maho arṇaḥ' — abundant water; that is, makes it known in an eminent way. Further, by her own form as a deity she 'virājati' — shines forth, illumines distinctly — all 'dhiyaḥ' — all the understandings of the performers; the understanding concerned with performance; the sense is: she produces them all." The final clause, "sarvotpādayatīty arthaḥ," is printed as given; It is read as continuing the sentence, and the sense is a little loose.

सरस्वत्या द्विरूपत्वं यास्को दर्शयति । तत्र सरस्वतीत्येतस्य नदीवद्देवतावच्च निगमा भवन्ति । नि. २-२३ । इति । एकशतसंख्याकेषूदकनामसु अर्णः क्षोद इति पठितम् । एतामृचं यास्को व्याचष्ट । महदर्णः सरस्वती प्रचेतयति प्रज्ञापयति केतुना कर्मणा प्रज्ञया वेमानि च सर्वाणि प्रज्ञानान्यभिविराजति । नि. ११-२१ । इति ॥ sarasvatyā dvirūpatvaṃ yāsko darśayati | tatra sarasvatīty etasya nadīvad devatāvac ca nigamā bhavanti | ni. 2-23 [?] | iti | ekaśata-saṃkhyākeṣūdaka-nāmasv arṇaḥ kṣoda iti paṭhitam | etām ṛcaṃ yāsko vyācaṣṭa | mahad arṇaḥ sarasvatī pracetayati prajñāpayati ketunā karmaṇā prajñayā vemāni ca sarvāṇi prajñānāny abhivirājati | ni. 11-27 | iti ||

Translation: "Yāska shows the twofold nature of Sarasvatī: 'Of this "Sarasvatī" the Vedic passages are both river-like and deity-like' (Nirukta 2-23 [?]). Among the hundred-and-one names of water, 'arṇaḥ' and 'kṣodaḥ' are read. Yāska explains this Ṛk thus: 'Sarasvatī makes known a great flood ("arṇaḥ"), by her action, and by her wisdom she shines over all these kinds of knowledge.' (Nirukta 11-27)."

Grammar within the Bhāṣya characterized, sūtras kept: "Mahaḥ" — "mahat" with the final "t" turned into "s" by vyatyaya (Vedic licence), then "ru" → "ḥ"; the accent of the bare stem falls on its last syllable. एङः पदान्तादति (eṅaḥ padāntād ati, पा. ६-१-१०९) would give the preceding form ("pūrvarūpa"), but by प्रकृत्यान्तःपादमव्यपरे (prakṛtyāntaḥpādam avyapare, पा. ६-१-११५) the natural form is retained within the pāda. "Arṇaḥ" — from "ṛ," the Uṇādi affix "asun" (उ. ४-१९६), with the augment "nuṭ," and "ṛ" taking guṇa. "Ketunā" — the accent of the bare stem is on the last syllable. "Viśvāḥ" — "viśva" has the first syllable acute, as it ends in the affix "kvan" (क्वन् [?]). The print here closes the Bhāṣya with the marks "॥ ६ ॥ ॥ १ ॥" — these are read as the varga-end marks; the verse-number ॥१२॥ itself is printed at the end of the grammar on p. 85.

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥

सरस्वती (sarasvatī) — the river Sarasvatī | केतुना (ketunā) — by an action in the form of flowing (by flowing) | महो अर्णः (maho arṇaḥ) — very abundant water | प्र चेतयति (pra cetayati) — makes known in an eminent way | (और) विश्वाः धियः (viśvāḥ dhiyaḥ) — (and) the understanding (the wisdom) of all people (devoted to sacrifice and rites) | वि राजति (vi rājati) — illumines. Page header: "Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya-sahitā · Maṇḍala 1, Anuvāka 1, Sūkta 3." English as printed in the source.

original p. 84

Rik 3.12: Bhāvārtha, English rendering; Special topics (opening)

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥

Since the river Sarasvatī flows with a very deep current, there is a great deal of water in this river; and this goddess also illumines the minds of those who praise her or who worship her by sacrifice — that is, she impels people's understanding so that it becomes keen.

English Translation (printed in English in the source itself):

"Saraswati (river) manifests herself by her acts (flowing) as a mighty river and (in her own form) enlightens peoples's [sic] minds."

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥

This mantra is used in the sacrifice called Sautrāmaṇī, for praising Sarasvatī. Yāska has explained this Ṛk in his Nirukta as follows — "mahad arṇaḥ sarasvatī pracetayati prajñāpayati ketunā karmaṇā prajñayā vemāni ca sarvāṇi prajñānāny abhivirājati" (महदर्णः सरस्वती प्रचेतयति प्रज्ञापयति केतुना कर्मणा प्रज्ञया वेमानि च सर्वाणि प्रज्ञानान्यभिविराजति — Ni. 11-27). Both the river form and the form of the goddess of speech of Sarasvatī Yāska states in the passage "tatra sarasvatīty etasya nadīvad devatāvac ca nigamā bhavanti" (तत्र सरस्वतीत्येतस्य नदीवद्देवतावच्च निगमा भवन्ति — Ni. 2-23). In this Ṛk, in the first half — that is, in the first two pādas — Sarasvatī is regarded and praised as being of river form, and in the third pāda as being of the form of a deity.

महो अर्णः (maho arṇaḥ) — The word "arṇa" is read among the hundred-and-one [print: "101"] names that indicate water. "Arṇa" means "water" and also "river." Here, although the river Sarasvatī was not a large river like the Sindhu and others, the praise of her as "maho arṇaḥ" — a big river with abundant floods — is right, we may say: for when one is praising, it is customary in the world to magnify and extol even a little of the quality that a deity has; moreover, the ṛṣi of this Ṛk, Madhucchanda, may have seen no large rivers such as the Sindhu, being far from them. It is therefore natural that he praises this river as a very large river, with abundant water in it.

केतुना (ketunā) — The Bhāṣyakāra and Yāska both explain this as "karmaṇā" — "by action." When it is explained as relating to the river, "ketunā" means "by the flow (of the nature of a figure of speech, rūpaka-karma)," so deep and so abundant; and when explained as relating to the deity, it may mean "by the action that stirs (impels) the minds of people." The deep, endless and impetuous flood of the river Sarasvatī (the source's English: "Saraswati's mighty, endless and impetuous flood") is described in many mantras, such as Ṛ. Saṃ. 6-6[?]-1[?] [?]. For this word Western scholars give "Brightness, banner, flag, activity, wisdom." Skandasvāmī gives for "ketunā" … "by the action that is of the nature of a roar (garjanā)…" Page header: "Aṣṭaka 1, Adhyāya 1, Varga 6 · Ṛgveda-saṃhitā." Grammar characterized, sūtras kept.

original p. 85

Special topics on Rik 3.12 (concluded); Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā; end of Sūkta 3

Continuing "ketunā" from p. 84: …Skandasvāmī, that is, explains "ketunā" as "by the action of roaring"; Yāska explains it as "karmaṇā prajñayā vā" ("by action, or by wisdom"). The view of Uvvaṭa and Mahīdhara is the same as Skandasvāmī's. Veṅkaṭamādhava gives for "ketunā" only "karmaṇā."

धियः (dhiyaḥ) — "Buddhi, ālocanā" (understanding, reflection). Yāska and Skandasvāmī (in the sense of) "prajñā" and "karman"; Veṅkaṭamādhava, "prajñā"; Uvvaṭa and Mahīdhara, "buddhi." Among Western scholars, Grassmann gives "act of devotion," and another scholar name not legible in the print "Devotion, thought" .

विराजति (virājati) — The Bhāṣyakāra explains it as "viśeṣeṇa dīpayati" ("illumines in a special way") — that is, "causes to shine greatly, impels, kindles." For this word, which is the third person singular of the root "rāj," the senses "shine, preside, govern, brighten" may be given. "Dhiyo virājati" means "she impels the minds to engage in good works," or "she makes our minds contented."

॥ Vyākaraṇa-prakriyā ॥ "Maho arṇaḥ": the "t" of "mahat" becomes "s" by vyatyaya (Vedic licence); for the "s," ससजुषो रुः (sasajuṣo ruḥ, पा. ८-२-६६) gives "ru"; for "ru," रुग्तोरोरुप्लुतादप्लुते (ato ror aplutād aplute, पा. ६-१-११३) gives "u"; "mah + u"; then अदुग्णे [print; I read it as the guṇa rule आद्गुणः (ād guṇaḥ), पा. ६-१-८७, but the print differs, and I do not alter it] gives guṇa → "maho." When it joins the word "arṇaḥ," एङः पदान्तादति (पा. ६-१-१०९) would produce the preceding form, but प्रकृत्यान्तःपादमव्यपरे (पा. ६-१-११५) keeps the natural form for "e/o" at the end of a word inside a pāda, when a short "a" follows, and not "v/y" (the print: when a "va" or "ya" follows after the short vowel, this does not apply); so, the natural form is retained, and we have "maho arṇaḥ." "Arṇaḥ" — from the root "ṛ gatau" ("ṛ, to go": "it flows, goes" — "arṇaḥ"); when the sense "water" is intended, the Uṇādi-sūtra उदके नुट् च (udake nuṭ ca, उ. सू. ४-१९६ [?]) — after "ṛ," "asun" with the augment "nuṭ"; with them, "ṛ + nas" → guṇa → "ar + nas"; by रषाभ्यां नो णः समानपदे (पा. ८-४-१) the "n" becomes "ṇ"; "ru"-substitution and visarga: "arṇaḥ." "Ketunā" — from the stem-accent it is end-acute. "Viśvāḥ" — "viśva" is formed with the "kvan" affix and is first-syllable acute. ॥१२॥

Sūkta 4 — "surūpakṛtnum ūtaye"

original p. 86

Sūkta 4: title; Sāyaṇa's introduction; the Anuvāda (opening)

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥

प्रथमे मण्डले द्वितीयेऽनुवाके चत्वारि सूक्तानि । तत्र सुरूपेत्यादिकं दशर्चं प्रथमं सूक्तं सुरूपकृत्नुं दशेत्यनुक्रान्तत्वात् । पूर्वस्मान्मधुच्छन्दसो गायत्रस्य चानुवृत्तेरस्य एवर्षिश्छन्दसी । इन्द्रं पृच्छेति चतुर्थ्यामृचि लिङ्गदर्शनादिन्द्रो देवता । अभिप्लवषडहे ब्राह्मणाच्छंसिनः प्रातःसवने स्तोमवृद्ध्यावापार्थानि सुरूपकृत्नुमूतय इत्यादीनि षट् सूक्तानि । सूत्रितं चाभिप्लवपृष्ठ्याहानीति खण्डे ब्राह्मणाच्छंसिनः सुरूपकृत्नुमूतय इति षट् सूक्तानि । आ. ७-५ । इति । आद्यानि त्रीणि सूक्तानि महाव्रते निष्केवल्य औष्णिहतृचाशीतौ शस्तव्यानि । उक्तं च शौनकेन । सुरूपकृत्नुमूतय इति त्रीण्येन्द्र सानसिं रयिमिति सूक्ते । ऐ. आ. ५-२-५ । इति । चतुर्विंशेऽहनि माध्यन्दिने सवने ब्राह्मणाच्छंसिनः सुरूपकृत्नुमूतय इति वैकल्पिकः स्तोत्रियस्तृचः । होत्रकाणामिति खण्डे मदे मदे हि नो ददिः सुरूपकृत्नुमूतये । आ. ७-४ । इति सूत्रितत्वात् । अग्निष्टोमे वैश्वदेवशस्त्रे सुरूपकृत्नुमूतय इति धाय्या । सुरूपकृत्नुमूतये तक्षन्रथम् । आ. ५-१८ । इति सूत्रितत्वात् ॥ prathame maṇḍale dvitīye 'nuvāke catvāri sūktāni | tatra surūpetyādikaṃ daśarcaṃ prathamaṃ sūktaṃ surūpakṛtnuṃ daśety anukrāntatvāt | pūrvasmān madhucchandaso gāyatrasya cānuvṛtter asya evarṣi-cchandasī | indraṃ pṛccheti caturthyām ṛci liṅga-darśanād indro devatā | abhiplava-ṣaḍahe brāhmaṇācchaṃsinaḥ prātaḥ-savane stoma-vṛddhy-āvāpārthāni surūpakṛtnum ūtaya ity ādīni ṣaṭ sūktāni | sūtritaṃ cābhiplava-pṛṣṭhy-āhānīti khaṇḍe brāhmaṇācchaṃsinaḥ surūpakṛtnum ūtaya iti ṣaṭ sūktāni | ā. 7-5 | iti | ādyāni trīṇi sūktāni mahāvrate niṣkevalya auṣṇiha-tṛcāśītau śastavyāni | uktaṃ ca śaunakena | surūpakṛtnum ūtaya iti trīṇy endra sānasiṃ rayim iti sūkte | ai. ā. 5-2-5 | iti | caturviṃśe 'hani mādhyandine savane brāhmaṇācchaṃsinaḥ surūpakṛtnum ūtaya iti vaikalpikaḥ stotriyas tṛcaḥ | hotrakāṇām iti khaṇḍe made made hi no dadiḥ surūpakṛtnum ūtaye | ā. 7-4 | iti sūtritatvāt | agniṣṭome vaiśvadeva-śastre surūpakṛtnum ūtaya iti dhāyyā | surūpakṛtnum ūtaye takṣan ratham | ā. 5-18 | iti sūtritatvāt ||

Translation: "In the first Maṇḍala, in the second Anuvāka, there are four sūktas. Of these, the first, beginning 'surūpa…', is of ten Ṛks, as the Anukramaṇī has it: 'surūpakṛtnuṃ daśa.' Because of the continuation (anuvṛtti) from the preceding, the ṛṣi and metre of this one are the same — Madhucchandas, and Gāyatrī. By the evidence of the gender-mark in the fourth Ṛk, 'indraṃ pṛccha,' Indra is the deity. In the Abhiplava-ṣaḍaha (six-day rite), at the morning pressing, the six sūktas beginning 'surūpakṛtnum ūtaye' are (to be recited) by the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin for the increase and the insertion (āvāpa) of the stoma; and this is laid down in the sūtra, in the section 'abhiplava-pṛṣṭhy-āhāni': 'the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin's six sūktas beginning "surūpakṛtnum ūtaye"' (Āśv. [Śrauta-sūtra] 7-5). The first three of these sūktas are to be recited, in the Mahāvrata, as the niṣkevalya-śastra, together with an Auṣṇiha tṛca, in the 'aśīti' (the eighty-verse recitation). And it has been said by Śaunaka: 'surūpakṛtnum ūtaye — three; and the two sūktas "indra sānasiṃ rayim"' (Aitareya Āraṇyaka 5-2-5). On the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin's tṛca 'surūpakṛtnum ūtaye' is an optional stotriya tṛca; and in the section on the Hotrakas it is laid down: 'made made hi no dadiḥ, surūpakṛtnum ūtaye' (Āśv. 7-4). In the Agniṣṭoma, in the Vaiśvadeva-śastra, 'surūpakṛtnum ūtaye' is the dhāyyā (the 'placing' verse): 'surūpakṛtnum ūtaye; takṣan ratham' (Āśv. 5-18)."

॥ Anuvādaḥ ॥ Kannada commentary, translated

As we said earlier (see Ṛ. Saṃ. Part II, page 3 [?]), the three sūktas of the first anuvāka of the first Maṇḍala are finished. From here the second Anuvāka begins. In this anuvāka there are four sūktas — (1) "surūpakṛtnum ūtaye," (2) "ā tvetā niṣīdata," (3) "yuñjanti bradhnam aruṣam," (4) "indram id gāthino bṛhat." Each of these four sūktas has ten Ṛks. As for the preceding sūktas, the ṛṣi of all four of these sūktas is the same Madhucchandas Vaiśvāmitra; the deity of this sūkta is Indra. In the first three Ṛks no deity's name is explicitly given; but because in the fourth Ṛk the words "indraṃ pṛccha" are used, and since from there on in the 5th, 6th, 7th and 10th [?] Ṛks too the word "Indra" occurs, Indra is the deity of this whole sūkta. There is no rule that the deity's name must occur in all the Ṛks of a sūkta; where some Ṛks have it, the remaining Ṛks present that deity's subject, and so… continues on the next page Page header: "Aṣṭaka 1, Adhyāya 1, Varga 7 · Ṛgveda-saṃhitā."

original p. 87

Viniyoga of Sūkta 4; heading: ṛṣi, deity, metre; Rik 4.1 (Saṃhitā, Pada)

Continuing: …so the same deity must be said to apply to all the Ṛks of the sūkta. The order of application (viniyoga) of this sūkta is as follows. In the sacrifice called Abhiplava-ṣaḍaha, in the morning pressing, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin — the assistant ṛtvij of the Hotṛ — is to recite this sūkta "surūpakṛtnum ūtaye," together with the next five sūktas, for the increase of the stoma. In this regard, the sūtra: "sūtritaṃ cābhiplava-pṛṣṭhy-āhānīti khaṇḍe brāhmaṇācchaṃsinaḥ surūpakṛtnum ūtaya iti ṣaṭ sūktāni" (सूत्रितं चाभिप्लवपृष्ठ्याहानीति खण्डे ब्राह्मणाच्छंसिनः सुरूपकृत्नुमूतय इति षट् सूक्तानि — Āśv. Sū. 7-5). Of these six sūktas the first three are used in the rite called Mahāvrata as niṣkevalya-śastra mantras, as stated in the section "abhiplava-pṛṣṭhy-āhāni." Here Śaunaka has quoted the sentence of the Aitareya Āraṇyaka: "surūpakṛtnum ūtaya iti trīṇy endra sānasiṃ rayim iti sūkte" (Ai. Ā. 5-2-5) — that is, the three sūktas beginning "surūpakṛtnum ūtaye" and the two sūktas beginning "indra sānasiṃ rayim" are to be recited. Further, in the above-mentioned rite, on the twenty-fourth day, at the midday pressing, the Brāhmaṇācchaṃsin may optionally recite the tṛca "surūpakṛtnum ūtaye" (three Ṛks). The Āśvalāyana-sūtra says in the section "hotrakāṇām": "made made hi no dadiḥ surūpakṛtnum ūtaye" (Āśv. Sū. 7-4) — that the tṛca "made made hi no dadiḥ" (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-81-7) and the tṛca "surūpakṛtnum ūtaye" (1-4-1) are to be recited; and in the Agniṣṭoma, when reciting the Vaiśvadeva-śastra mantras — "surūpakṛtnum ūtaye" (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-4-1) and "takṣan rathaṃ suvṛtam" (Ṛ. Saṃ. 1-111-1) (Āśv. Sū. 5-18) — it is said in the Āśvalāyana sūtra that these Ṛks may be recited as special mantras.

॥ ओम् ॥

सूक्त—४ Sūkta 4 ॥ मण्डल—१ ॥ अनुवाक—२ ॥ सूक्त—४ ॥ ॥ अष्टक—१ ॥ अध्याय—१ ॥ वर्ग—७, ८ ॥ ॥ सूक्तदल्लिरुव ऋक्संख्ये १० ॥ number of Ṛks in the sūkta: 10 ऋषिः — मधुच्छन्दा वैश्वामित्रः (ṛṣiḥ — madhucchandā vaiśvāmitraḥ) देवता — इन्द्रः (devatā — indraḥ) छन्दः — गायत्री (chandaḥ — gāyatrī)

॥ Saṃhitā-pāṭhaḥ ॥ Page header: "Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya-sahitā · Maṇḍala 1, Anuvāka 2, Sūkta 4." Saṃhitā accents as printed; Pada unaccented. Sanskrit printed in Kannada script; [?] where unclear.

सु॒रू॒प॒कृत्नुमू॒तये॑ सु॒दुघा॑मिव गो॒दुहे॑ । जु॒हू॒मसि॒ द्यवि॑द्यवि ॥१॥

surūpakṛ́tnumūtáye sudúghāmiva godúhe | juhūmási dyávidyavi ||1||

original p. 88

Rik 4.1: Pada-pāṭha, Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya, grammar (characterized), Pada-meanings (opening)

॥ Pada-pāṭhaḥ ॥ Reading note: the print divides the compounds with marks read as "sudughām-iva" and "go-duhe," "dyavi-dyavi"; The divisions are given as read from the printed signs.

सुरूपकृत्नुम् । ऊतये । सुदुघाम्ऽइव । गोऽदुहे । जुहूमसि । द्यविऽद्यवि ॥१॥

॥ Sāyaṇa-bhāṣyam ॥

सुरूपकृत्नुं शोभनरूपोपेतस्य कर्मणः कर्तारमिन्द्रमूतयेऽस्मद्रक्षणार्थं द्यवि द्यवि प्रतिदिनं जुहूमसि । आह्वयामः । आह्वाने दृष्टान्तः । गोदुहे गोदुगर्थं सुदुघामिव सुष्ठु दोग्ध्रीं गामिव । यथा लोके गोर्दोग्धा दोहार्थं तस्याभिमुखेन दोहनीयां गामाह्वयति तद्वत् । वस्तोरित्यादिषु द्वादशसंख्याकेष्वहर्नामसु द्यविद्यवीति पठितम् । surūpakṛtnuṃ śobhana-rūpopetasya karmaṇaḥ kartāram indram ūtaye 'smad-rakṣaṇārthaṃ dyavi dyavi pratidinaṃ juhūmasi | āhvayāmaḥ | āhvāne dṛṣṭāntaḥ | goduhe go-dugarthaṃ sudughām iva suṣṭhu dogdhrīṃ gām iva | yathā loke gor dogdhā dohārthaṃ tasyābhimukhena dohanīyāṃ gām āhvayati tadvat | vastor ity ādiṣu dvādaśa-saṃkhyākeṣv ahar-nāmasu dyavidyavīti paṭhitam |

Translation: "'Surūpakṛtnum' — the doer of action endowed with beautiful form — Indra — we call, 'ūtaye' — for our protection — 'dyavi dyavi' — day by day. The illustration for the calling: 'goduhe' — for the milker of the cow ('go-dug'), 'sudughām iva' — like a good milch-cow ('suṣṭhu dogdhrī gauḥ'). As, in the world, the milker of a cow calls the cow that is to be milked, to face him, for the sake of the milking, so (we call Indra). Among the twelve names for 'day,' beginning with 'vastoḥ,' 'dyavidyavi' is read."

Grammar within the Bhāṣya (characterized, not transcribed line by line; every sūtra cited is kept): "Surūpakṛtnum": "karoti iti kṛtnuḥ" — the affix "knu" after "kṛ" and "hi" (कृहिभ्यां क्नुः, उ. सू. ३-३०); since "knu" is "k"-marked, the guṇa does not occur; the "t" is inserted, a Vedic usage; the compound's accent is on its last syllable. "Ūtaye": "av" (to protect) takes "ktin" in the Vedic list "ūti-yūti-jūti-sāti-hetī-kīrtayaś ca" (ऊतियूतिजूतिसातिहेतिकीर्तयश्च, पा. ३-३-९७), which is irregularly formed (nipātana) and has the end-acute. "Sudughām": "su" + "dugdhā"; the affix "kap" after "duh" (दुहः कब्घश्च, पा. ३-२-७०), and the "h" becomes "gh"; "kap" being "p"-marked, the accent of the root remains with the "u" acute. With "su" as a gati-compound, the second member's accent is retained; with "iva" the case-ending is not elided (इवेन विभक्त्यलोपः पूर्वपदप्रकृतिस्वरत्वं च, as on p. 58). "Goduhe": "gāṃ dogdhīti godhuk" — "kvip" in the sense of "doer" by सत्सूद्विषद्रुहदुहयुजविदभिदच्छिदजिनीराजामुपसर्गेऽपि क्विप् (पा. ३-२-६१); the accent of the second member of a kṛt compound is retained. "Juhūmasi": "hve" (hūyate) in the first-person plural laṭ; "śap" is replaced by "ślu" in the Veda (बहुलं छन्दसि, पा. २-४-७६); "samprasāraṇa" of the root before the doubling (अभ्यस्तस्य च, पा. ६-१-३३) and the "pūrvarūpa" (संप्रसारणाच्च, पा. ६-१-१०८); the lengthening (हलः, पा. ६-४-२); then the doubling by "ślau"; shortening of the reduplicative syllable (ह्रस्वः, पा. ७-४-५९); the "c"/"j" substitutions (चुत्वजश्त्वे, पा. ७-४-६२; ८-४-५४); the "mas" ending takes "i" by इदन्तो मसिः (पा. ७-१-४६); the "m" is acute by the accent of the affix. "Dyavi dyavi": "dyu" has the bare-stem accent on the last syllable; in the sense of repetition the word is doubled (नित्यवीप्सयोः, पा. ८-१-४); and the second is, by परमाम्रेडितम् (पा. ८-१-२) and अनुदात्तं च (पा. ८-१-३) [numbers as printed], unaccented.

॥ Prati-padārthaḥ ॥ Kannada, translated; continued on the next page

गोदुहे (goduhe) — for the sake of milking | सुदुघामिव (sudughām iva) — like a cow that gives milk (or that gives much milk) | सुरूपकृत्नुम् (surūpakṛtnum) — (him) who does good (beautiful) deeds — (Indra) … Page header: "Aṣṭaka 1, Adhyāya 1, Varga 7 · Ṛgveda-saṃhitā." English as printed in the source. The verse cited below is as printed; The same Ṛk was already quoted in Sūkta 3, p. 25 of this volume's earlier text.

original p. 89

Rik 4.1: Pada-meanings concluded; Bhāvārtha; English rendering; Special topics (opening)

…who does (Indra) | ऊतये (ūtaye) — for (our) protection | द्यविद्यवि (dyavidyavi) — every day | जुहूमसि (juhūmasi) — we call (we call him to come near us).

॥ Bhāvārthaḥ ॥ Kannada, translated

Just as we call, with love, a cow that gives milk, to come near us, so every day, for our protection, we call to us Indra, who can do wonderful — that is, daring — deeds.

English Translation (printed in English in the source itself):

"We invoke the performer of beautiful actions (Indra) day by day for our protection like a good milch-cow for the purpose of milking."

॥ Viśeṣa-viṣayagaḷu (Special Topics) ॥

सुरूपकृत्नुम् (surūpakṛtnum) — This word is not used elsewhere in the Ṛgveda than in this Ṛk. The Bhāṣyakāra explains this word as "śobhana-rūpopetasya karmaṇaḥ kartāram" ("the doer of action endowed with beautiful form") — one who does works of a good form. The explanation of Skandasvāmī and Veṅkaṭamādhava is the same. Griffith and Macdonell follow Sāyaṇa's sense. Grassmann, the German scholar: "He who knows to perform beautiful things" — one with the power to do beautiful deeds; Ludwig: "Creater [sic] of beautiful forms" — one who can create beautiful shapes. But Geldner: "when he assumes his good forms or he who shows himself from his best side" — "one who shows his own best form" — and in support of this meaning he has cited the Ṛk:

रूपंरूपं प्रतिरूपो बभूव तदस्य रूपं प्रतिचक्षणाय । इन्द्रो मायाभिः पुरुरूप ईयते युक्ता ह्यस्य हरयः शता दश ॥ (ऋ. सं. ६-४७-१८) rūpaṃ-rūpaṃ pratirūpo babhūva tad asya rūpaṃ praticakṣaṇāya | indro māyābhiḥ pururūpa īyate yuktā hy asya harayaḥ śatā daśa || (ṛ. saṃ. 6-47-18) The source's English (from Geldner): "He has become suitable to every form; this true form of his is to be recognised again and again. Indra assumes many forms by virtue of his mysterious power; for, ten hundred horses have been yoked for him."

— the chief import being that Indra, by his own power of māyā, is able to assume many forms. And… Page header: "Sāyaṇa-bhāṣya-sahitā · Maṇḍala 1, Anuvāka 2, Sūkta 4."
